text.description: The words, or the styling too. A plain string is shorthand for {"content": ...}; an object is a set_text patch merged over the Title preset. Text properties to merge. Keys: content, font (a PostScript name), size (px), color, align (left|center|right), valign (top|middle|bottom), line_spacing, tracking, outline (null or {width, color}), backdrop (null or {color, padding, radius}), width (null for auto-sizing, or a wrap width in px), animation (null or {kind: typewriter|word_fade|line_rise, in, out} — how the words arrive and leave. in and out are DURATIONS in ticks measured from the clip's own first and last frame, not times; either may be 0 for no ramp at that end, and in + out longer than the clip simply shows a partial reveal, and both are snapped to the document's frame grid. Like shadow and backdrop it MERGES: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {animation: null} clears the whole thing), case (as_written|upper — applied before layout; it never changes the word count), words (one {start, end} per whitespace token of content, in clip ticks, or [] for an untimed page — a content change that alters the count must send words: [] in the same patch), word_style (null or {mode: highlight|build, active_color, active_scale 1–1.5, active_pill {color, padding, radius, glide}, spoken_color, upcoming_color, active_fill, pause_dim 0–1} — how the word being said is drawn; it replaces animation. Three looks, each off by default: active_pill.glide (true|false) slides the pill from the word before to the active one over 0.2 s, or sooner when the next word starts sooner, instead of jumping; active_fill (true|false) fills the active word left to right from its start to its end, taking 0.6 s at most — the part said in active_color and the rest in upcoming_color, or not yet drawn in build mode; in highlight mode it shows only where those two colours differ; pause_dim fades the words and the pill to 1 − pause_dim of their opacity in a pause of 0.25 s or more — after one word's end until the next one's start, before a late first word, and after the last word until the clip ends — over 0.1 s each way, and outside 0–1 it is refused). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped. Default: the Title preset's placeholder.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_track
tools.description: Adds an empty track. INDEX 0 IS THE BACK of the layer stack — the bottom lane of the timeline, drawn first — and tracks.count is the front, which is what ⇧⌘N adds and where an overlay belongs.

index.description: Where in the stack (0 = back). Default: the front.

name.description: Track name, e.g. "Titles".

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_transition
tools.description: Makes an overlap at the HARD CUT before a clip and puts a transition on it — Clip ▸ Transition ▸ <kind> on a clip that abuts the one before it. The overlap is built out of material the two clips already have (the source before the incoming clip's in point, and after the outgoing clip's out point), so NOTHING else on the timeline moves and the pair's outer edges stay exactly where they were. duration is snapped down to whole frames and CLAMPED — to each side's available material, to the neighbours on the track, and to the overlap rule — so a request too long for the media lands shorter rather than failing; a request that clamps below one frame is refused. An affected track already outside the overlap rule is refused by that rule before fitting. align center takes half from each side (an odd frame goes to the incoming clip, and a side with nothing to give passes its share to the other), before takes it all from the incoming clip's head, after all from the outgoing clip's tail. kind absent uses the clip's stored kind if it has one and cross_dissolve otherwise; a stored transition keeps its curve and crossfade, a new one is eased at both ends and crossfades its sound. The incoming clip's actions move with its new first frame, so a zoom stays on the source frame it was drawn over. Errors when duration is not positive and when the clip is NOT at a hard cut, naming which of: no clip before it, a gap, an overlap that already exists (use set_transition or set_transition_duration for that one). With ripple true the overlap is made by MOVING instead — the sheet's Shift Clips Left button when neither clip has footage beyond the cut: no material is read and align is ignored, and the incoming clip plus every clip at or after the cut on every unlocked track slides left by duration, so the timeline gets that much shorter and no clip's source window changes. It is capped at half the shorter of the two clips and limited to the greatest whole-frame shift that leaves every moved track inside the overlap rule, including after clips cross; a clip on another track pushed into its neighbour gets a cross_dissolve; markers do not move.

align.description: Which side the overlap comes out of. Default center. Ignored with ripple.

duration.description: Requested overlap length, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Clamped, never refused for being too long.

kind.description: The transition. Absent uses the clip's stored kind, else cross_dissolve. Not nullable — set_transition clears.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

ripple.description: Make the overlap by sliding the incoming clip and everything after it left, for two clips with no footage beyond the cut. Default false.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_graphic
tools.description: Reads the project's graphics/ folder. With name: that module's source, revision (the SHA-256 of its bytes), path, whether it compiles (ok, meta, schema, diagnostics), the clips drawn by it and kept, the revisions of its kept earlier texts, newest first (restore_graphic takes one). Without: folder, the folder's absolute path — where it WILL be when folder_exists is false; the first write_graphic creates it — and every module with its revision, ok and clips, warnings: what the folder's scan skipped or could not watch, in its own sentences, and history: [{name, kept}] for every name with a kept text, deleted modules included. The folder may also be edited with your own file tools: modules (<name>.js), fonts in fonts/ (.ttf, .otf) and pictures in assets/; the app sees a change within a moment. API.md and API.d.ts there are the reference, written by the app, and history/ is the app's too: the kept texts, which restore_graphic reads.

name.description: The module to read. Omit for the folder.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_project
tools.description: The whole project as JSON: canvas (width, height, fps [num, den], background, fit_new_clips, timecode_frames), media, tracks, clips and markers, with next_id — the schema every op edits. Plus the state that is deliberately NOT in the model and lives only in the app: playhead, selection and the in/out range. Read this first: every other tool names things by the ids it reports, and clip, track, marker and media ids share ONE number space, so an id is unambiguous on its own. tracks[0] is the BACK of the layer stack (the bottom lane of the timeline); times are ticks at 600000 per second. missing_media lists media whose file has moved — relink_media points it at the new one. graphics: every module in the package's graphics/ with its revision, whether it compiles, and the clips drawn by it.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__graphic_reference
tools.description: Answers the whole graphics API — the module's shape, ctx, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, limits and idioms — as Markdown, for an LLM to read once before writing a graphic. Needs no project open; a project, when given, must name an open one. Help ▸ Graphics Reference opens the same file.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_frame
tools.description: Renders one frame of the finished timeline as a picture so you can SEE the result — the verification hook. It goes through the same composition and the same Metal compositor an export does, so this is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it. The image comes back both as an image block and as a file on disk whose path the text names. Use it before and after every edit. It writes a PNG to a temporary file unless path or format says otherwise, so a call that names neither is exactly the call it always was. When a graphic in the frame warned or failed, a sentence before the last names the graphic, its frame and the diagnostic; a failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

format.description: The container to write. Default: the path's own extension when it is one of those (.jpg counts as jpeg), else png — so a call with no path and no format writes a PNG, as it always has. An explicit format WINS and the path's extension is REPLACED rather than appended to, so {path: "shot.jpg", format: "png"} writes shot.png. png and heic keep the canvas's alpha; JPEG has no alpha channel: a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

histogram.description: Also measure the frame's histogram, View ▸ Scopes' Histogram: R′, G′, B′ and Y′ counts per 256 levels. The text says what share of pixels clips high and low by Y′, and <image path>.histogram.json holds the four planes' counts and both percentages. Default false.

max_width.description: Cap the image's width in px, aspect kept and never upscaled. Default: the canvas's own size.

parade.description: Also measure the frame's RGB parade, View ▸ Scopes' Parade: R′, G′ and B′ each binned as the waveform bins Y′. The text says what share of pixels each channel clips high and low, and <image path>.parade.json holds the counts keyed red, green and blue (each 256 arrays by column bin, indexed by level) with each channel's clip marks and clip counts. Default false.

path.description: Where to write the file, e.g. ~/Desktop/shot.png. The folder must exist. Omit for a temporary file; either way the text block's last sentence names the file that was written. This is the same writer File ▸ Save Frame... uses, so a PNG written here and one saved from the menu are byte-identical.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

selection.description: An adjustment clip's id: draw what its video.qualifier selects instead of grading — grey, white fully graded, black untouched, times any matte cutting it, its strength not applied — with every layer in front of it left out; black where the clip is not on the frame. View ▸ Show Selection's picture; the view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Refused unless it names an adjustment clip. Default: none.

t.description: The moment to render, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default: the playhead.

ungraded.description: Render as if no clip were graded — every clip's video.color (Light and Color) neutral, everything else kept: View ▸ Show Ungraded's picture. The view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Default false.

vectorscope.description: Also measure the frame's vectorscope, View ▸ Scopes' Vectorscope: Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral (bin 128). The text says what share of pixels is neutral, and <image path>.vectorscope.json holds the counts (256 arrays by Cr bin, indexed by Cb bin), the six 75 % targets' bins and the skin line's angle. Default false.

waveform.description: Also measure the frame's luma waveform, View ▸ Scopes' Waveform: the text says what share of pixels clips high and low, and <image path>.waveform.json holds the 256 × 256 counts (one array per column bin, indexed by level), the clip marks and both percentages. Default false.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_graphic
tools.description: Renders a module in graphics/ WITHOUT a clip — to look at it before placing it. png (the default) answers a contact sheet: the frames on a grid, each frame number printed under its cell, the cells scaled down (never the gaps or labels) so the sheet fits max_width; plus one sentence per frame that failed (drawn as its error card) or warned, with the engine's location. svg answers one frame's SVG text, its diagnostics and the ctx it was drawn with. ctx is a clip's: the canvas fps, durationInFrames from meta (else 5 s), the size from width/height, else meta, else the canvas. svg takes no path, background or max_width, which are the png sheet's, and writes no file. A frame at or past durationInFrames is drawn, with progress 1, as a longer clip draws it. A png sheet draws at most 134217728 px of frames (frames × width × height); past that the call is refused before any frame is drawn. No inspector control mirrors it: a person looks at the preview well.

background.description: What the png sheet is painted on: transparent (the default), checker, or a hex colour (#rgb, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa). Not with format svg.

format.description: png (default): the contact sheet. svg: one frame's SVG text.

frame.description: One frame to draw. Not with frames.

frames.description: The frames to draw, 1 to 16 of them, in order. Not with frame. Omit both for frame 0.

height.description: Height to draw at, in pixels. Default: meta.height, else the canvas.

max_width.description: The widest the png sheet may be, in pixels. Default 2048; 8192 keeps a 1920-wide graphic's two cells at full size. Not with format svg.

name.description: The module: graphics/<name>.js.

path.description: Where to write the png sheet; its folder must exist. Omit for a temporary file. The reply ends "Written to <path>." Not with format svg.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

props.description: The values to draw with, keyed by the schema's names; a key left out draws with the schema's default.

width.description: Width to draw at, in pixels. Default: meta.width, else the canvas.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__save_project
tools.description: Saves the project. A project that has never been saved — a new_project with no path, or a movie opened as one — needs a path; passing a path always writes there (Save As). text.description: The words, or the styling too. A plain string is shorthand for {"content": ...}; an object is a set_text patch merged over the Title preset. Text properties to merge. Keys: content, font (a PostScript name), size (px), color, align (left|center|right), valign (top|middle|bottom), line_spacing, tracking, outline (null or {width, color}), backdrop (null or {color, padding, radius}), width (null for auto-sizing, or a wrap width in px), animation (null or {kind: typewriter|word_fade|line_rise, in, out} — how the words arrive and leave. in and out are DURATIONS in ticks measured from the clip's own first and last frame, not times; either may be 0 for no ramp at that end, and in + out longer than the clip simply shows a partial reveal, and both are snapped to the document's frame grid. Like shadow and backdrop it MERGES: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {animation: null} clears the whole thing), case (as_written|upper — applied before layout; it never changes the word count), words (one {start, end} per whitespace token of content, in clip ticks, or [] for an untimed page — a content change that alters the count must send words: [] in the same patch), word_style (null or {mode: highlight|build, active_color, active_scale 1–1.5, active_pill {color, padding, radius, glide}, spoken_color, upcoming_color, active_fill, pause_dim 0–1} — how the word being said is drawn; it replaces animation. Three looks, each off by default: active_pill.glide (true|false) slides the pill from the word before to the active one over 0.2 s, or sooner when the next word starts sooner, instead of jumping; active_fill (true|false) fills the active word left to right from its start to its end, taking 0.6 s at most — the part said in active_color and the rest in upcoming_color, or not yet drawn in build mode; in highlight mode it shows only where those two colours differ; pause_dim fades the words and the pill to 1 − pause_dim of their opacity in a pause of 0.25 s or more — after one word's end until the next one's start, before a late first word, and after the last word until the clip ends — over 0.1 s each way, and outside 0–1 it is refused). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped. Default: the Title preset's placeholder.

entries.name: mcp__framejob__add_transition
entries.description: Makes an overlap at the HARD CUT before a clip and puts a transition on it — Clip ▸ Transition ▸ <kind> on a clip that abuts the one before it. The overlap is built out of material the two clips already have (the source before the incoming clip's in point, and after the outgoing clip's out point), so NOTHING else on the timeline moves and the pair's outer edges stay exactly where they were. duration is snapped down to whole frames and CLAMPED — to each side's available material, to the neighbours on the track, and to the overlap rule — so a request too long for the media lands shorter rather than failing; a request that clamps below one frame is refused. An affected track already outside the overlap rule is refused by that rule before fitting. align center takes half from each side (an odd frame goes to the incoming clip, and a side with nothing to give passes its share to the other), before takes it all from the incoming clip's head, after all from the outgoing clip's tail. kind absent uses the clip's stored kind if it has one and cross_dissolve otherwise; a stored transition keeps its curve and crossfade, a new one is eased at both ends and crossfades its sound. The incoming clip's actions move with its new first frame, so a zoom stays on the source frame it was drawn over. Errors when duration is not positive and when the clip is NOT at a hard cut, naming which of: no clip before it, a gap, an overlap that already exists (use set_transition or set_transition_duration for that one). With ripple true the overlap is made by MOVING instead — the sheet's Shift Clips Left button when neither clip has footage beyond the cut: no material is read and align is ignored, and the incoming clip plus every clip at or after the cut on every unlocked track slides left by duration, so the timeline gets that much shorter and no clip's source window changes. It is capped at half the shorter of the two clips and limited to the greatest whole-frame shift that leaves every moved track inside the overlap rule, including after clips cross; a clip on another track pushed into its neighbour gets a cross_dissolve; markers do not move.

entries.name: mcp__framejob__get_graphic
entries.description: Reads the project's graphics/ folder. With name: that module's source, revision (the SHA-256 of its bytes), path, whether it compiles (ok, meta, schema, diagnostics), the clips drawn by it and kept, the revisions of its kept earlier texts, newest first (restore_graphic takes one). Without: folder, the folder's absolute path — where it WILL be when folder_exists is false; the first write_graphic creates it — and every module with its revision, ok and clips, warnings: what the folder's scan skipped or could not watch, in its own sentences, and history: [{name, kept}] for every name with a kept text, deleted modules included. The folder may also be edited with your own file tools: modules (<name>.js), fonts in fonts/ (.ttf, .otf) and pictures in assets/; the app sees a change within a moment. API.md and API.d.ts there are the reference, written by the app, and history/ is the app's too: the kept texts, which restore_graphic reads.

entries.name: mcp__framejob__get_project
entries.description: The whole project as JSON: canvas (width, height, fps [num, den], background, fit_new_clips, timecode_frames), media, tracks, clips and markers, with next_id — the schema every op edits. Plus the state that is deliberately NOT in the model and lives only in the app: playhead, selection and the in/out range. Read this first: every other tool names things by the ids it reports, and clip, track, marker and media ids share ONE number space, so an id is unambiguous on its own. tracks[0] is the BACK of the layer stack (the bottom lane of the timeline); times are ticks at 600000 per second. missing_media lists media whose file has moved — relink_media points it at the new one. graphics: every module in the package's graphics/ with its revision, whether it compiles, and the clips drawn by it.

Needs no project open; a project, when given, must name an open one. Help ▸ Graphics Reference opens the same file.

entries.name: mcp__framejob__render_frame
entries.description: Renders one frame of the finished timeline as a picture so you can SEE the result — the verification hook. It goes through the same composition and the same Metal compositor an export does, so this is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it. The image comes back both as an image block and as a file on disk whose path the text names. Use it before and after every edit. It writes a PNG to a temporary file unless path or format says otherwise, so a call that names neither is exactly the call it always was. When a graphic in the frame warned or failed, a sentence before the last names the graphic, its frame and the diagnostic; a failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

format.description: The container to write. Default: the path's own extension when it is one of those (.jpg counts as jpeg), else png — so a call with no path and no format writes a PNG, as it always has. An explicit format WINS and the path's extension is REPLACED rather than appended to, so {path: "shot.jpg", format: "png"} writes shot.png. png and heic keep the canvas's alpha; JPEG has no alpha channel: a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

histogram.description: Also measure the frame's histogram, View ▸ Scopes' Histogram: R′, G′, B′ and Y′ counts per 256 levels. The text says what share of pixels clips high and low by Y′, and <image path>.histogram.json holds the four planes' counts and both percentages. Default false.

max_width.description: Cap the image's width in px, aspect kept and never upscaled. Default: the canvas's own size.

The text says what share of pixels each channel clips high and low, and <image path>.parade.json holds the counts keyed red, green and blue (each 256 arrays by column bin, indexed by level) with each channel's clip marks and clip counts. A frame at or past durationInFrames is drawn, with progress 1, as a longer clip draws it. A png sheet draws at most 134217728 px of frames (frames × width × height); past that the call is refused before any frame is drawn. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

content.text:
# Frame Job graphics — the API

A **graphic** is a motion graphic drawn by code: one JavaScript ES module
whose `render` returns an SVG string for each frame. Frame Job runs it in a
sandboxed QuickJS engine and rasterizes the SVG with resvg. The same frame
with the same props always draws the same pixels. This page is the whole
API. Every `js` block on it is run by a test, so the examples work as
written.

## The module

```js
export const meta = {
  name: "Lower third",        // shown in the inspector
  durationInFrames: 150,      // optional: the default length of a new clip
};

export const schema = {
  title:    { type: "string",  default: "Jane Doe", label: "Title" },
  subtitle: { type: "string",  default: "Director of Photography" },
  accent:   { type: "color",   default: "#ff5a36" },
  size:     { type: "number",  default: 64, min: 12, max: 200, step: 1 },
  boxed:    { type: "boolean", default: true },
  align:    { type: "enum",    default: "left", options: ["left", "center", "right"] },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [-600, 96], { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true });
  const fade = interpolate(frame, [ctx.durationInFrames - 15, ctx.durationInFrames - 1], [1, 0],
    { clamp: true });
  const y = ctx.height - 200;
  return svg(ctx, `
    <g opacity="${fade}">
      ${props.boxed ? `<rect x="${x}" y="${y - 90}" width="700" height="150" fill="#101014"/>` : ""}
      <rect x="${x}" y="${y - 90}" width="12" height="150" fill="${props.accent}"/>
      <text x="${x + 40}" y="${y}" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="800"
            font-size="${props.size}" fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(props.title)}</text>
    </g>`);
}
```

- `render(frame, props, ctx)` is required. It must return a string that
  starts with `<svg`; use `svg(ctx, body)` to write the root element.
- `meta` is optional (`{}` when absent). `name` and `durationInFrames` are
  read from it.
- `schema` is optional (`{}` when absent). It declares the props (below).
- The module is the only source of code: no `import`, no `eval`, no
  `Function`. The standard library below is already global.
- `frame` is an integer counted from the clip's first frame.

## `ctx`

| key | what |
|---|---|
| `fps` | the project's frame rate, e.g. `30` or `29.97002997` |
| `time` | `frame / fps`, in seconds |
| `durationInFrames` | the clip's length in frames |
| `progress` | `frame / max(1, durationInFrames - 1)`, clamped to 0–1 |
| `width`, `height` | the graphic's size in pixels |
| `canvas` | `{width, height}`, the project's canvas |

Write every coordinate in terms of `ctx.width` and `ctx.height` (or a unit
such as `const u = ctx.height / 1080`) so the graphic draws at any size.

## The schema

At most 64 keys. A key is letters, digits and `_`, starts with a letter or
`_`, and is at most 32 characters. Every entry needs a `type` and a
`default` of that type; `label` (else the key) and `help` (a tooltip) are
optional. Any entry may say `animate: false` (a boolean; absent is `true`):
an action never animates that prop, and the inspector writes it to the clip
even while an action is selected — for a count, a layout mode or a data
series a ramp would break.

| `type` | value | options |
|---|---|---|
| `string` | text, at most 4096 characters | `multiline: true` for a text area |
| `number` | a finite number | `min`, `max`, `step` |
| `boolean` | `true` / `false` | |
| `color` | a CSS colour string: `"#ff5a36"`, `"rgb(255, 90, 54)"`, `"hsl(11, 100%, 61%)"`, `"tomato"` | |
| `enum` | one of `options` | `options`: 1–32 strings |
| `asset` | a file name in `graphics/assets/`, `null` or `""` (no image); `render` gets `null` for either of the last two | `kind: "image"` |

A schema that breaks a rule does not compile, and the error says which rule.
A `color` entry's `default` must be a colour in the grammar
`interpolateColors` lists below, or the module does not compile:
`schema.accent.default "bluish" is not a color`. `props` receives the
default as written, not normalised.
`props` always has every schema key: a stored value replaces the default
only when it fits the type. A value that does not fit is a WARNING, the
default is drawn, and the frame still draws, e.g.
`props.size is a string but the schema says number; the default 64 is used`.

## The standard library

### `svg(ctx, body, {background})`

The root element with the right `width`, `height` and `viewBox`.

```js
const plain = svg(ctx, `<circle cx="100" cy="100" r="50" fill="#fff"/>`);
const onBlack = svg(ctx, "", { background: "#000000" });
```

### `interpolate(value, input, output, {easing, clamp, extrapolateLeft, extrapolateRight})`

Maps `value` through matching `input` and `output` ranges (two or more
points, `input` ascending). Outside `input` it extends the end segment
unless `clamp: true`; `extrapolateLeft` / `extrapolateRight` take
`"extend"`, `"clamp"` or `"identity"`.

```js
const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 400], { clamp: true });
const pulse = interpolate(frame, [0, 15, 30], [1, 1.2, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutSine });
```

### `Easing`

`Easing.linear`, `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, and `in`, `out` and `inOut`
of `quad`, `cubic`, `quart`, `expo`, `sine`, `back` and `elastic`, spelled
`Easing.inQuad`, `Easing.outCubic`, `Easing.inOutBack` and so on. Each takes
`t` in 0–1 and is exact at 0 and 1.

```js
const eased = Easing.outCubic(0.5);
const custom = Easing.bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)(0.5);
const y = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [300, 0], { easing: Easing.outBack, clamp: true });
```

### `spring({frame, fps, stiffness = 100, damping = 10, mass = 1, from = 0, to = 1})`

A physical spring from `from` to `to`, starting at frame 0 (use
`frame - delay` to start later). It overshoots unless damped. The same frame
always answers the same value.

```js
const scale = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 14 });
const late = spring({ frame: frame - 12, fps: ctx.fps, stiffness: 180, from: 0.5, to: 1 });
```

### `interpolateColors(value, input, colors)`

Blends colours in OKLab and answers `#rrggbb` (or `#rrggbbaa` when a colour
has alpha). Clamped outside `input`. A colour is `#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`,
`#rrggbbaa`, `rgb()` / `rgba()` (channels 0–255 or a percentage, alpha 0–1
or a percentage), `hsl()` / `hsla()` (hue in degrees, saturation and
lightness percentages), or one of the 147 CSS colour names or
`transparent` — the same colours a `color` prop takes. A value out of range
(`rgb(300, 0, 0)`) throws rather than being clamped.

```js
const fill = interpolateColors(frame, [0, 60], ["#ff5a36", "#3666ff"]);
const glass = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["rgba(255, 255, 255, 0)", "#ffffff"]);
const sky = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["hsl(200, 80%, 30%)", "skyblue"]);
```

### `random(seed)`

A number in [0, 1) that depends only on `seed` (a number or a string).
`Math.random` does not exist in a graphic; this replaces it.

```js
const jitter = random(`dot-${frame}`) * 10;
const hue = Math.floor(random(42) * 360);
```

### `noise2D(seed, x, y)` and `noise3D(seed, x, y, z)`

Simplex noise in about −1..1. Use `noise3D` with time as the third axis for
smooth drift.

```js
const drift = noise2D("wave", frame / 60, 0) * 40;
const wobble = noise3D(7, 0.5, 0.5, ctx.time) * 20;
```

### Paths: `getLength(d)`, `getPointAtLength(d, length)` and `evolvePath(progress, d)`

`d` is SVG path data: every command (`M L H V C S Q T A Z`) and its
relative form. `getLength` answers the path's length, curves and arcs
measured to within about 0.01 %. `getPointAtLength` answers `{x, y, angle}`:
the point that far along the path (`length` is clamped to the path) and the
way the path is heading there, in degrees, ready for `rotate()`.
`evolvePath` answers `{strokeDasharray, strokeDashoffset}` for a `progress`
of 0–1: put both on the `<path>` and it is drawn from its start up to that
fraction. Its dash is 0.1 % longer than the measured length, so a closed
outline closes at 1.

A path of several pieces (more than one `M`) draws them all at once, each
from its own start and at the same speed, the longest finishing at 1; pieces
drawn one after another are one `<path>` each. A path that cannot be read
throws, naming where reading stopped —
`getLength: cannot parse the path at character 6: "X 5 5"` — and is never a
silent zero. A number too large to do arithmetic with (`1e999`, or a line
1e200 long, whose square overflows) is refused in the same sentence, so no
answer is ever `Infinity` or `NaN`.

The paths a graphic measures are remembered, so the same `d` costs a lookup
on later calls and frames — up to 32 paths, and about 50,000 characters and
measured pieces between them (a curve is 64 pieces). Past either limit all
are forgotten and measured again when next asked for, so with paths that
large take every length and point from one before turning to the next.

```js
const d = `M 200 ${ctx.height / 2} C 600 100 1000 900 1400 ${ctx.height / 2}`;
const total = getLength(d);
const tip = getPointAtLength(d, total * ctx.progress);
const dash = evolvePath(ctx.progress, d);
const line = `<path d="${d}" fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="8"
  stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
  <circle cx="${tip.x}" cy="${tip.y}" r="12" fill="#ffcc00"/>`;
```

### `measureText(text, font)`

`font` is `{family, size, weight, style, letterSpacing, xmlSpace}`
(defaults Montserrat, 16, 400, `"normal"`, 0, `"default"`). Answers
`{width, ascent, descent, lineHeight, inkX, inkWidth}`: `width` is the
advance (where the next word starts); `inkX` / `inkWidth` are the drawn
glyphs. With `xmlSpace: "default"` runs of spaces collapse as SVG draws
them; with `"preserve"` a run of spaces beside a drawn glyph counts, as
`xml:space="preserve"` draws it, and any other value throws. Text that is
only whitespace measures zero either way. A family that is not installed
throws, naming the families that are.

```js
const m = measureText("Hello", { family: "Montserrat", size: 64, weight: 800 });
const boxWidth = m.width + 80;
const gap = measureText("a  b", { family: "sans-serif", size: 48, xmlSpace: "preserve" });
```

### `wrapText(text, maxWidth, font)`

Lines that each fit `maxWidth`; a word longer than the width breaks by
characters.

```js
const lines = wrapText("A title long enough to need two lines", 600,
  { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 64, weight: 700 });
```

### `fitText(text, maxWidth, font, {min = 8, max = 400})`

The largest whole font size at which `text` fits `maxWidth` on one line.

```js
const size = fitText("BREAKING", ctx.width - 200, { family: "Anton" }, { max: 300 });
```

### `textLines(lines, {x, y, lineHeight, anchor, fill, font})`

A `<text>` with one `<tspan>` per line, the family QUOTED for you (a CSS
generic such as `sans-serif` is written bare, as it must be).
`anchor` is `"start"`, `"middle"` or `"end"`; `lineHeight` defaults to
1.2 × the size. A font with `xmlSpace: "preserve"` writes
`xml:space="preserve"` on the `<text>`, so it draws the spaces `measureText`
counted; a `style` of `"italic"` or `"oblique"` and a non-zero
`letterSpacing` are written as `font-style` and `letter-spacing`, so it draws
the font `wrapText` broke the lines with.

```js
const font = { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 48, weight: 600 };
const body = textLines(wrapText("Two short lines of text", 400, font),
  { x: 100, y: 200, anchor: "start", fill: "#ffffff", font });
const code = textLines(["let  x = 1;"],
  { x: 100, y: 300, font: { family: "monospace", size: 32, xmlSpace: "preserve" } });
```

### `escapeXml(s)`

Escapes `& < > " '` — put every prop you write into markup through it.

```js
const safe = escapeXml("Tom & Jerry <live>");
```

### `formatNumber(n, {decimals = 0, separator = ","})`

There is no `Intl` in the engine; this groups thousands.

```js
const label = formatNumber(1234567.891, { decimals: 2 });
const plain = formatNumber(Math.round(interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, 5000], { clamp: true })));
```

### `asset(name)`

The href for a file in the project's `graphics/assets/` folder, for
`<image href="…">`. A name that is not there is a warning naming the files
that are; the image then does not draw.

An asset's name must not start with `.` or `#`, must hold none of
`/ : " ' < > &` and no control character, and is at most 247 bytes. A
picture added under any other name is renamed as it is copied in —
`#logo&mark.png` becomes `logo-mark.png`, then `logo-mark-2.png` if that is
taken — and you are told the name to use. A file put in the folder by hand
under such a name is skipped, with a warning.

```js
const logo = `<image href="${asset("logo.png")}" x="40" y="40" width="200" height="200"/>`;
```

## Fonts

A graphic draws with the fonts bundled with Frame Job, plus any `.ttf` /
`.otf` in the project's `graphics/fonts/`. Never the system's.

| family | weights |
|---|---|
| Anton | 400 |
| Bebas Neue | 400 |
| Darker Grotesque | variable, 300–900 |
| IBM Plex Mono | 400, 500 |
| Montserrat | 800, 900 |
| Source Sans 3 | variable, 200–900 |
| Source Serif 4 | variable, 200–900 |

The CSS generic families draw in bundled faces: `serif` is Source Serif 4,
`sans-serif` is Source Sans 3 and `monospace` is IBM Plex Mono. Write a
generic unquoted (`font-family="sans-serif"`); quoted, it names a family
called "sans-serif", which is not installed. `cursive` and `fantasy` are not
installed.

**Quote a family** in `font-family` or the `font` shorthand when any word
of it starts with a digit: `font-family="'Source Sans 3'"`,
`font: 48px 'Source Sans 3'`. Unquoted, `Source Sans 3` is not a
valid family list: it draws nothing, with a warning. `textLines` quotes
for you. A family the set lacks draws nothing, with a warning naming the
families that are installed; in a list (`"Nope, Montserrat"`) the first
installed family draws.

## The sandbox

A graphic is a pure function of `frame`, `props`, `ctx` and its fonts and
assets. These refuse, with these sentences:

```text
Math.random()        → Math.random is not available; use random(seed)
import x from "x"    → imports are not available in a graphic; the standard library is global
new Function("…")    → Function is not available in a graphic; the module is the one source of code
eval("…")            → ReferenceError: eval is not defined
```

`Date` is frozen: `Date.now()` is `946684800000` and `new Date()` is
2000-01-01T00:00:00Z. There is no `fetch`, file, clock, `performance`,
`WebAssembly` or `Intl`. Modern syntax works: template literals, `??`, `?.`,
`**`, destructuring, `Array.prototype.at`, `replaceAll`, `findLast`.

## Limits

- **Time**: each call has a budget — 250 ms per frame in preview, 2 s in an
  export. The module's top level has one too. Over it, the answer is an
  error such as `over the 250 ms budget at frame 12 (InternalError:
  interrupted)`.
- **Memory**: 64 MB of heap and 1 MB of stack per engine. Past either is an
  error with a line and column.
- **Size**: a graphic draws at most 8192 pixels on a side.
- **The answer**: `render` must return an SVG string. `undefined` is
  ``render returned undefined at frame 12 — did you forget `return`?``.
  The string may be at most 8 MiB (8388608 bytes); a longer one is
  `render returned 9000000 bytes at frame 12; the SVG may be at most
  8388608 bytes`.

## Diagnostics

Every problem comes back as `{level, message, line, column, frame}`.
`level` is `"error"` (nothing drew) or `"warning"` (it drew anyway).
`line` and `column` are the module's own, when known; for a timeout they
are where the function begins, not the statement that ran long. `frame` is
set for a problem found while drawing. A warning from the module's top level
(such as `asset("x")` outside `render`) has no frame, and comes back with the
module's compile: `ok` is still `true`.

## Working over MCP

Read `graphic_reference` once. `write_graphic {name, source}` answers `ok` and
`diagnostics`: write again until `ok` is true. `render_graphic {name, frames}`
draws up to 16 frames on a contact sheet with no clip, at most 134217728
pixels of frames in all (two at 8192×8192, or sixteen at 3840×2160);
`add_graphic_clip {name}` places it, `render_frame` shows a frame,
`set_graphic {patch: {props}}` changes it.
`paste_attributes {clips, payload, groups: ["graphic"]}` copies one clip's props onto other clips
drawn by the same module. `import_graphic_font {path}` answers `families`, the exact names
`font-family` must say; `import_graphic_asset {path}` adds a picture for
`asset(name)`; its `name` is the one to use, and `renamed_from` says it was
renamed. `get_graphic` reads a module or names the folder, which your file
tools may edit too; its `API.md` is this page, `API.d.ts` its types.
`get_graphic {}`'s `warnings` says what the folder's scan skipped or could
not watch, such as a file whose name is not a module name. The app keeps the
last 10 texts of each module whenever it sees one replaced: `kept`, in
`write_graphic`'s and `get_graphic {name}`'s answers, lists their revisions,
newest first, and `get_graphic {}`'s `history` lists every name with a kept
text, deleted modules included. `restore_graphic {name, revision?}` writes a
kept text back (the newest by default) and keeps the one it replaced.
`delete_graphic {name}` removes a module no clip draws and keeps its text, so
`restore_graphic` brings it back. `rename_graphic {name, to}` renames a
module and repoints every clip that draws it as one undo step; undo renames
the file back. The folder's `history/` is the app's: leave it to those three
tools. A successful
`export` answers `graphic_warnings`, each distinct warning a graphic gave
while the file was drawn, with its name and frame.

## Animating a prop from the timeline

A graphic clip's props can be the target of an action, as a clip's position or opacity can:
`add_action {clip, at, duration}` makes the span, and `set_action_end {clip, action, patch:
{graphic: {props: {…}}}}` names the values the props end at. Each value is checked against your
schema as `set_graphic` checks it, `min` and `max` included, using the module as it is now. Across
the action a `number` and a `color` ramp along its curve, a `color` in OKLab, giving the same middle
`interpolateColors` gives; a `string`, `boolean` and `enum` change to the end's value when the
action ends, and an `asset` changes to the end's image when the action ends, `""` naming no image
there (a `null` stops animating the prop); a prop whose entry says `animate: false` cannot be
animated (`set_action_end` refuses a value for it). A prop the clip holds no value
for starts from the schema's `default` as it is when an action first names it, and that value is
written into the clip, so a later change to the default does not move the animation; an asset
whose default is `null` starts from `""`. `render` gets
that frame's values every frame, and your own animation from `frame` still runs on top. A `null`
for a prop in `set_action_end`'s patch stops animating it.

**An animated number arrives with decimals**: 64 to 129 is 96.5 halfway, never rounded and never
snapped to `step`. A module that needs a whole number rounds it itself, or marks the prop
`animate: false` so no action ramps it. One that does neither —
`new Array(props.count)` is the usual case — throws on a fraction, so those frames draw the error
card, and an export stops there.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Bars", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = {
  count: { type: "number", default: 5, min: 1, max: 20, step: 1 },
  accent: { type: "color", default: "#ff5a36" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const n = Math.round(props.count);
  const w = ctx.width / (2 * n);
  let bars = "";
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    bars += `<rect x="${(2 * i + 0.5) * w}" y="${ctx.height / 3}" width="${w}"
      height="${ctx.height / 3}" fill="${props.accent}"/>`;
  }
  return svg(ctx, bars);
}
```

A colour blends in OKLab with straight alpha, exactly as `interpolateColors` blends it: `#ff0000`
to `#0000ff` is `#8c53a2` halfway, not the muddy `#800080` of a channel-by-channel blend, and
`#ffffff` to `#00000000` is `#63636380`, grey and half transparent. While a prop
moves, every frame is drawn anew, so a graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the
length of the action.

## Video inside a graphic: the matte

A graphic cannot read a video's pixels. To show video inside a shape the graphic draws, put the
graphic on the track directly above the video and switch that track to a **matte**: Track ▸ Matte
in the app, or `set_track {track, matte}` over MCP. A matte track's clips are never drawn. What
they show cuts the track directly behind: with `alpha`, the video shows where the graphic is
opaque; with `alpha_inverted`, where it is transparent; with `luma` and `luma_inverted`, by the
brightness of what it draws. `matte: "none"` turns it off. Where the matte track has no clip, the
video shows uncut. The module is written and called exactly as anywhere else. Fill the window in
white so it works in every mode, and animate it as usual: the cut follows each frame.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Window", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { radius: { type: "number", default: 24, min: 0, max: 200 } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const t = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 18 });
  const w = ctx.width * 0.6 * t;
  const h = ctx.height * 0.6 * t;
  return svg(ctx, `<rect x="${(ctx.width - w) / 2}" y="${(ctx.height - h) / 2}"
    width="${w}" height="${h}" rx="${props.radius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`);
}
```

On a matte track a clip's position, scale, opacity, crop and actions still shape the window. Its
blend mode, drop shadow and reflection do nothing. The matted video's own drop shadow follows the
cut-out shape.

## Idioms

### A slide-in

```js
export const meta = { name: "Slide in", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { text: { type: "string", default: "Hello" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const u = ctx.height / 1080;
  const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 18], [-ctx.width / 2, ctx.width / 2],
    { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true });
  return svg(ctx, `<text x="${x}" y="${ctx.height / 2}" text-anchor="middle"
    font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="800" font-size="${120 * u}"
    fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(props.text)}</text>`);
}
```

### A staggered list

```js
export const meta = { name: "Agenda" };
export const schema = {
  items: { type: "string", default: "Intro\nDemo\nQuestions", multiline: true, animate: false },
  accent: { type: "color", default: "#ffcc00" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const u = ctx.height / 1080;
  const rows = props.items.split("\n").filter((s) => s.trim()).map((item, i) => {
    const t = spring({ frame: frame - i * 6, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 16 });
    const y = 300 * u + i * 110 * u;
    return `<g opacity="${Math.min(1, t)}" transform="translate(${(1 - t) * 80 * u} 0)">
      <rect x="${160 * u}" y="${y - 50 * u}" width="${14 * u}" height="${64 * u}" fill="${props.accent}"/>
      <text x="${200 * u}" y="${y}" font-family="'Source Sans 3'" font-weight="600"
        font-size="${64 * u}" fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(item)}</text></g>`;
  });
  return svg(ctx, rows.join(""));
}
```

### A counter

```js
export const meta = { name: "Counter", durationInFrames: 120 };
export const schema = {
  to: { type: "number", default: 25000, min: 0 },
  suffix: { type: "string", default: " views" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const value = interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, props.to], { easing: Easing.outExpo, clamp: true });
  const text = formatNumber(Math.round(value)) + props.suffix;
  return svg(ctx, `<text x="${ctx.width / 2}" y="${ctx.height / 2}" text-anchor="middle"
    font-family="'IBM Plex Mono'" font-weight="500" font-size="${ctx.height / 8}"
    fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(text)}</text>`);
}
```

### Fit and wrap a title

```js
export const meta = { name: "Title card" };
export const schema = {
  title: { type: "string", default: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const maxWidth = ctx.width * 0.8;
  const base = { family: "Bebas Neue", weight: 400 };
  const size = fitText(props.title, maxWidth * 2, base, { min: 48, max: 220 });
  const font = Object.assign({}, base, { size });
  const lines = wrapText(props.title, maxWidth, font);
  const top = ctx.height / 2 - (lines.length - 1) * size * 0.6;
  const fade = interpolate(frame, [0, 12], [0, 1], { clamp: true });
  return svg(ctx, `<g opacity="${fade}">${textLines(lines,
    { x: ctx.width / 2, y: top, anchor: "middle", fill: "#ffffff", font })}</g>`,
    { background: "#16161a" });
}
```

### A draw-on stroke

`evolvePath` measures the path and answers the dash that draws it up to a
progress of 0–1.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Underline", durationInFrames: 60 };
export const schema = { color: { type: "color", default: "#ff5a36" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const y = ctx.height * 0.62;
  const d = `M ${ctx.width * 0.2} ${y} q ${ctx.width * 0.3} ${ctx.height * 0.05} ${ctx.width * 0.6} 0`;
  const drawn = interpolate(frame, [0, 24], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutCubic, clamp: true });
  const dash = evolvePath(drawn, d);
  return svg(ctx, `<path d="${d}" stroke="${props.color}"
    stroke-width="${ctx.height / 90}" stroke-linecap="round" fill="none"
    stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>`);
}
```

### Follow a path

`getPointAtLength` answers where the path is and which way it is heading;
`rotate(angle)` turns an arrowhead drawn pointing right to match.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Arrow", durationInFrames: 60 };
export const schema = { color: { type: "color", default: "#ffffff" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const w = ctx.width;
  const h = ctx.height;
  const d = `M ${w * 0.2} ${h * 0.7} C ${w * 0.4} ${h * 0.2} ${w * 0.6} ${h * 0.2} ${w * 0.8} ${h * 0.5}`;
  const drawn = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutCubic, clamp: true });
  const dash = evolvePath(drawn, d);
  const tip = getPointAtLength(d, getLength(d) * drawn);
  const s = h / 36;
  return svg(ctx, `<path d="${d}" stroke="${props.color}" stroke-width="${h / 120}" fill="none"
    stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
    <path d="M ${-s} ${-s * 0.6} L ${s * 0.5} 0 L ${-s} ${s * 0.6} Z" fill="${props.color}"
    transform="translate(${tip.x} ${tip.y}) rotate(${tip.angle})"/>`);
}
```

# Frame Job graphics — the API

A **graphic** is a motion graphic drawn by code: one JavaScript ES module
whose `render` returns an SVG string for each frame. Frame Job runs it in a
sandboxed QuickJS engine and rasterizes the SVG with resvg. The same frame
with the same props always draws the same pixels. This page is the whole
API. Every `js` block on it is run by a test, so the examples work as
written.

## The module

```js
export const meta = {
  name: "Lower third",        // shown in the inspector
  durationInFrames: 150,      // optional: the default length of a new clip
};

export const schema = {
  title:    { type: "string",  default: "Jane Doe", label: "Title" },
  subtitle: { type: "string",  default: "Director of Photography" },
  accent:   { type: "color",   default: "#ff5a36" },
  size:     { type: "number",  default: 64, min: 12, max: 200, step: 1 },
  boxed:    { type: "boolean", default: true },
  align:    { type: "enum",    default: "left", options: ["left", "center", "right"] },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [-600, 96], { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true });
  const fade = interpolate(frame, [ctx.durationInFrames - 15, ctx.durationInFrames - 1], [1, 0],
    { clamp: true });
  const y = ctx.height - 200;
  return svg(ctx, `
    <g opacity="${fade}">
      ${props.boxed ? `<rect x="${x}" y="${y - 90}" width="700" height="150" fill="#101014"/>` : ""}
      <rect x="${x}" y="${y - 90}" width="12" height="150" fill="${props.accent}"/>
      <text x="${x + 40}" y="${y}" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="800"
            font-size="${props.size}" fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(props.title)}</text>
    </g>`);
}
```

- `render(frame, props, ctx)` is required. It must return a string that
  starts with `<svg`; use `svg(ctx, body)` to write the root element.
- `meta` is optional (`{}` when absent). `name` and `durationInFrames` are
  read from it.
- `schema` is optional (`{}` when absent). It declares the props (below).
- The module is the only source of code: no `import`, no `eval`, no
  `Function`. The standard library below is already global.
- `frame` is an integer counted from the clip's first frame.

## `ctx`

| key | what |
|---|---|
| `fps` | the project's frame rate, e.g. `30` or `29.97002997` |
| `time` | `frame / fps`, in seconds |
| `durationInFrames` | the clip's length in frames |
| `progress` | `frame / max(1, durationInFrames - 1)`, clamped to 0–1 |
| `width`, `height` | the graphic's size in pixels |
| `canvas` | `{width, height}`, the project's canvas |

Write every coordinate in terms of `ctx.width` and `ctx.height` (or a unit
such as `const u = ctx.height / 1080`) so the graphic draws at any size.

## The schema

At most 64 keys. A key is letters, digits and `_`, starts with a letter or
`_`, and is at most 32 characters. Every entry needs a `type` and a
`default` of that type; `label` (else the key) and `help` (a tooltip) are
optional. Any entry may say `animate: false` (a boolean; absent is `true`):
an action never animates that prop, and the inspector writes it to the clip
even while an action is selected — for a count, a layout mode or a data
series a ramp would break.

| `type` | value | options |
|---|---|---|
| `string` | text, at most 4096 characters | `multiline: true` for a text area |
| `number` | a finite number | `min`, `max`, `step` |
| `boolean` | `true` / `false` | |
| `color` | a CSS colour string: `"#ff5a36"`, `"rgb(255, 90, 54)"`, `"hsl(11, 100%, 61%)"`, `"tomato"` | |
| `enum` | one of `options` | `options`: 1–32 strings |
| `asset` | a file name in `graphics/assets/`, `null` or `""` (no image); `render` gets `null` for either of the last two | `kind: "image"` |

A schema that breaks a rule does not compile, and the error says which rule.
A `color` entry's `default` must be a colour in the grammar
`interpolateColors` lists below, or the module does not compile:
`schema.accent.default "bluish" is not a color`. `props` receives the
default as written, not normalised.
`props` always has every schema key: a stored value replaces the default
only when it fits the type. A value that does not fit is a WARNING, the
default is drawn, and the frame still draws, e.g.
`props.size is a string but the schema says number; the default 64 is used`.

## The standard library

### `svg(ctx, body, {background})`

The root element with the right `width`, `height` and `viewBox`.

```js
const plain = svg(ctx, `<circle cx="100" cy="100" r="50" fill="#fff"/>`);
const onBlack = svg(ctx, "", { background: "#000000" });
```

### `interpolate(value, input, output, {easing, clamp, extrapolateLeft, extrapolateRight})`

Maps `value` through matching `input` and `output` ranges (two or more
points, `input` ascending). Outside `input` it extends the end segment
unless `clamp: true`; `extrapolateLeft` / `extrapolateRight` take
`"extend"`, `"clamp"` or `"identity"`.

```js
const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 400], { clamp: true });
const pulse = interpolate(frame, [0, 15, 30], [1, 1.2, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutSine });
```

### `Easing`

`Easing.linear`, `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, and `in`, `out` and `inOut`
of `quad`, `cubic`, `quart`, `expo`, `sine`, `back` and `elastic`, spelled
`Easing.inQuad`, `Easing.outCubic`, `Easing.inOutBack` and so on. Each takes
`t` in 0–1 and is exact at 0 and 1.

```js
const eased = Easing.outCubic(0.5);
const custom = Easing.bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)(0.5);
const y = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [300, 0], { easing: Easing.outBack, clamp: true });
```

### `spring({frame, fps, stiffness = 100, damping = 10, mass = 1, from = 0, to = 1})`

A physical spring from `from` to `to`, starting at frame 0 (use
`frame - delay` to start later). It overshoots unless damped. The same frame
always answers the same value.

```js
const scale = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 14 });
const late = spring({ frame: frame - 12, fps: ctx.fps, stiffness: 180, from: 0.5, to: 1 });
```

### `interpolateColors(value, input, colors)`

Blends colours in OKLab and answers `#rrggbb` (or `#rrggbbaa` when a colour
has alpha). Clamped outside `input`. A colour is `#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`,
`#rrggbbaa`, `rgb()` / `rgba()` (channels 0–255 or a percentage, alpha 0–1
or a percentage), `hsl()` / `hsla()` (hue in degrees, saturation and
lightness percentages), or one of the 147 CSS colour names or
`transparent` — the same colours a `color` prop takes. A value out of range
(`rgb(300, 0, 0)`) throws rather than being clamped.

```js
const fill = interpolateColors(frame, [0, 60], ["#ff5a36", "#3666ff"]);
const glass = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["rgba(255, 255, 255, 0)", "#ffffff"]);
const sky = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["hsl(200, 80%, 30%)", "skyblue"]);
```

### `random(seed)`

A number in [0, 1) that depends only on `seed` (a number or a string).
`Math.random` does not exist in a graphic; this replaces it.

```js
const jitter = random(`dot-${frame}`) * 10;
const hue = Math.floor(random(42) * 360);
```

### `noise2D(seed, x, y)` and `noise3D(seed, x, y, z)`

Simplex noise in about −1..1. Use `noise3D` with time as the third axis for
smooth drift.

```js
const drift = noise2D("wave", frame / 60, 0) * 40;
const wobble = noise3D(7, 0.5, 0.5, ctx.time) * 20;
```

### Paths: `getLength(d)`, `getPointAtLength(d, length)` and `evolvePath(progress, d)`

`d` is SVG path data: every command (`M L H V C S Q T A Z`) and its
relative form. `getLength` answers the path's length, curves and arcs
measured to within about 0.01 %. `getPointAtLength` answers `{x, y, angle}`:
the point that far along the path (`length` is clamped to the path) and the
way the path is heading there, in degrees, ready for `rotate()`.
`evolvePath` answers `{strokeDasharray, strokeDashoffset}` for a `progress`
of 0–1: put both on the `<path>` and it is drawn from its start up to that
fraction. Its dash is 0.1 % longer than the measured length, so a closed
outline closes at 1.

A path of several pieces (more than one `M`) draws them all at once, each
from its own start and at the same speed, the longest finishing at 1; pieces
drawn one after another are one `<path>` each. A path that cannot be read
throws, naming where reading stopped —
`getLength: cannot parse the path at character 6: "X 5 5"` — and is never a
silent zero. A number too large to do arithmetic with (`1e999`, or a line
1e200 long, whose square overflows) is refused in the same sentence, so no
answer is ever `Infinity` or `NaN`.

The paths a graphic measures are remembered, so the same `d` costs a lookup
on later calls and frames — up to 32 paths, and about 50,000 characters and
measured pieces between them (a curve is 64 pieces). Past either limit all
are forgotten and measured again when next asked for, so with paths that
large take every length and point from one before turning to the next.

```js
const d = `M 200 ${ctx.height / 2} C 600 100 1000 900 1400 ${ctx.height / 2}`;
const total = getLength(d);
const tip = getPointAtLength(d, total * ctx.progress);
const dash = evolvePath(ctx.progress, d);
const line = `<path d="${d}" fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="8"
  stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
  <circle cx="${tip.x}" cy="${tip.y}" r="12" fill="#ffcc00"/>`;
```

### `measureText(text, font)`

`font` is `{family, size, weight, style, letterSpacing, xmlSpace}`
(defaults Montserrat, 16, 400, `"normal"`, 0, `"default"`). Answers
`{width, ascent, descent, lineHeight, inkX, inkWidth}`: `width` is the
advance (where the next word starts); `inkX` / `inkWidth` are the drawn
glyphs. With `xmlSpace: "default"` runs of spaces collapse as SVG draws
them; with `"preserve"` a run of spaces beside a drawn glyph counts, as
`xml:space="preserve"` draws it, and any other value throws. Text that is
only whitespace measures zero either way. A family that is not installed
throws, naming the families that are.

```js
const m = measureText("Hello", { family: "Montserrat", size: 64, weight: 800 });
const boxWidth = m.width + 80;
const gap = measureText("a  b", { family: "sans-serif", size: 48, xmlSpace: "preserve" });
```

### `wrapText(text, maxWidth, font)`

Lines that each fit `maxWidth`; a word longer than the width breaks by
characters.

```js
const lines = wrapText("A title long enough to need two lines", 600,
  { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 64, weight: 700 });
```

### `fitText(text, maxWidth, font, {min = 8, max = 400})`

The largest whole font size at which `text` fits `maxWidth` on one line.

```js
const size = fitText("BREAKING", ctx.width - 200, { family: "Anton" }, { max: 300 });
```

### `textLines(lines, {x, y, lineHeight, anchor, fill, font})`

A `<text>` with one `<tspan>` per line, the family QUOTED for you (a CSS
generic such as `sans-serif` is written bare, as it must be).
`anchor` is `"start"`, `"middle"` or `"end"`; `lineHeight` defaults to
1.2 × the size. A font with `xmlSpace: "preserve"` writes
`xml:space="preserve"` on the `<text>`, so it draws the spaces `measureText`
counted; a `style` of `"italic"` or `"oblique"` and a non-zero
`letterSpacing` are written as `font-style` and `letter-spacing`, so it draws
the font `wrapText` broke the lines with.

```js
const font = { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 48, weight: 600 };
const body = textLines(wrapText("Two short lines of text", 400, font),
  { x: 100, y: 200, anchor: "start", fill: "#ffffff", font });
const code = textLines(["let  x = 1;"],
  { x: 100, y: 300, font: { family: "monospace", size: 32, xmlSpace: "preserve" } });
```

### `escapeXml(s)`

Escapes `& < > " '` — put every prop you write into markup through it.

```js
const safe = escapeXml("Tom & Jerry <live>");
```

### `formatNumber(n, {decimals = 0, separator = ","})`

There is no `Intl` in the engine; this groups thousands.

```js
const label = formatNumber(1234567.891, { decimals: 2 });
const plain = formatNumber(Math.round(interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, 5000], { clamp: true })));
```

### `asset(name)`

The href for a file in the project's `graphics/assets/` folder, for
`<image href="…">`. A name that is not there is a warning naming the files
that are; the image then does not draw.

An asset's name must not start with `.` or `#`, must hold none of
`/ : " ' < > &` and no control character, and is at most 247 bytes. A
picture added under any other name is renamed as it is copied in —
`#logo&mark.png` becomes `logo-mark.png`, then `logo-mark-2.png` if that is
taken — and you are told the name to use. A file put in the folder by hand
under such a name is skipped, with a warning.

```js
const logo = `<image href="${asset("logo.png")}" x="40" y="40" width="200" height="200"/>`;
```

## Fonts

A graphic draws with the fonts bundled with Frame Job, plus any `.ttf` /
`.otf` in the project's `graphics/fonts/`. Never the system's.

| family | weights |
|---|---|
| Anton | 400 |
| Bebas Neue | 400 |
| Darker Grotesque | variable, 300–900 |
| IBM Plex Mono | 400, 500 |
| Montserrat | 800, 900 |
| Source Sans 3 | variable, 200–900 |
| Source Serif 4 | variable, 200–900 |

The CSS generic families draw in bundled faces: `serif` is Source Serif 4,
`sans-serif` is Source Sans 3 and `monospace` is IBM Plex Mono. Write a
generic unquoted (`font-family="sans-serif"`); quoted, it names a family
called "sans-serif", which is not installed. `cursive` and `fantasy` are not
installed.

**Quote a family** in `font-family` or the `font` shorthand when any word
of it starts with a digit: `font-family="'Source Sans 3'"`,
`font: 48px 'Source Sans 3'`. Unquoted, `Source Sans 3` is not a
valid family list: it draws nothing, with a warning. `textLines` quotes
for you. A family the set lacks draws nothing, with a warning naming the
families that are installed; in a list (`"Nope, Montserrat"`) the first
installed family draws.

## The sandbox

A graphic is a pure function of `frame`, `props`, `ctx` and its fonts and
assets. These refuse, with these sentences:

```text
Math.random()        → Math.random is not available; use random(seed)
import x from "x"    → imports are not available in a graphic; the standard library is global
new Function("…")    → Function is not available in a graphic; the module is the one source of code
eval("…")            → ReferenceError: eval is not defined
```

`Date` is frozen: `Date.now()` is `946684800000` and `new Date()` is
2000-01-01T00:00:00Z. There is no `fetch`, file, clock, `performance`,
`WebAssembly` or `Intl`. Modern syntax works: template literals, `??`, `?.`,
`**`, destructuring, `Array.prototype.at`, `replaceAll`, `findLast`.

## Limits

- **Time**: each call has a budget — 250 ms per frame in preview, 2 s in an
  export. The module's top level has one too. Over it, the answer is an
  error such as `over the 250 ms budget at frame 12 (InternalError:
  interrupted)`.
- **Memory**: 64 MB of heap and 1 MB of stack per engine. Past either is an
  error with a line and column.
- **Size**: a graphic draws at most 8192 pixels on a side.
- **The answer**: `render` must return an SVG string. `undefined` is
  ``render returned undefined at frame 12 — did you forget `return`?``.
  The string may be at most 8 MiB (8388608 bytes); a longer one is
  `render returned 9000000 bytes at frame 12; the SVG may be at most
  8388608 bytes`.

## Diagnostics

Every problem comes back as `{level, message, line, column, frame}`.
`level` is `"error"` (nothing drew) or `"warning"` (it drew anyway).
`line` and `column` are the module's own, when known; for a timeout they
are where the function begins, not the statement that ran long. `frame` is
set for a problem found while drawing. A warning from the module's top level
(such as `asset("x")` outside `render`) has no frame, and comes back with the
module's compile: `ok` is still `true`.

## Working over MCP

Read `graphic_reference` once. `write_graphic {name, source}` answers `ok` and
`diagnostics`: write again until `ok` is true. `render_graphic {name, frames}`
draws up to 16 frames on a contact sheet with no clip, at most 134217728
pixels of frames in all (two at 8192×8192, or sixteen at 3840×2160);
`add_graphic_clip {name}` places it, `render_frame` shows a frame,
`set_graphic {patch: {props}}` changes it.
`paste_attributes {clips, payload, groups: ["graphic"]}` copies one clip's props onto other clips
drawn by the same module. `import_graphic_font {path}` answers `families`, the exact names
`font-family` must say; `import_graphic_asset {path}` adds a picture for
`asset(name)`; its `name` is the one to use, and `renamed_from` says it was
renamed. `get_graphic` reads a module or names the folder, which your file
tools may edit too; its `API.md` is this page, `API.d.ts` its types.
`get_graphic {}`'s `warnings` says what the folder's scan skipped or could
not watch, such as a file whose name is not a module name. The app keeps the
last 10 texts of each module whenever it sees one replaced: `kept`, in
`write_graphic`'s and `get_graphic {name}`'s answers, lists their revisions,
newest first, and `get_graphic {}`'s `history` lists every name with a kept
text, deleted modules included. `restore_graphic {name, revision?}` writes a
kept text back (the newest by default) and keeps the one it replaced.
`delete_graphic {name}` removes a module no clip draws and keeps its text, so
`restore_graphic` brings it back. `rename_graphic {name, to}` renames a
module and repoints every clip that draws it as one undo step; undo renames
the file back. The folder's `history/` is the app's: leave it to those three
tools. A successful
`export` answers `graphic_warnings`, each distinct warning a graphic gave
while the file was drawn, with its name and frame.

## Animating a prop from the timeline

A graphic clip's props can be the target of an action, as a clip's position or opacity can:
`add_action {clip, at, duration}` makes the span, and `set_action_end {clip, action, patch:
{graphic: {props: {…}}}}` names the values the props end at. Each value is checked against your
schema as `set_graphic` checks it, `min` and `max` included, using the module as it is now. Across
the action a `number` and a `color` ramp along its curve, a `color` in OKLab, giving the same middle
`interpolateColors` gives; a `string`, `boolean` and `enum` change to the end's value when the
action ends, and an `asset` changes to the end's image when the action ends, `""` naming no image
there (a `null` stops animating the prop); a prop whose entry says `animate: false` cannot be
animated (`set_action_end` refuses a value for it). A prop the clip holds no value
for starts from the schema's `default` as it is when an action first names it, and that value is
written into the clip, so a later change to the default does not move the animation; an asset
whose default is `null` starts from `""`. `render` gets
that frame's values every frame, and your own animation from `frame` still runs on top. A `null`
for a prop in `set_action_end`'s patch stops animating it.

**An animated number arrives with decimals**: 64 to 129 is 96.5 halfway, never rounded and never
snapped to `step`. A module that needs a whole number rounds it itself, or marks the prop
`animate: false` so no action ramps it. One that does neither —
`new Array(props.count)` is the usual case — throws on a fraction, so those frames draw the error
card, and an export stops there.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Bars", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = {
  count: { type: "number", default: 5, min: 1, max: 20, step: 1 },
  accent: { type: "color", default: "#ff5a36" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const n = Math.round(props.count);
  const w = ctx.width / (2 * n);
  let bars = "";
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    bars += `<rect x="${(2 * i + 0.5) * w}" y="${ctx.height / 3}" width="${w}"
      height="${ctx.height / 3}" fill="${props.accent}"/>`;
  }
  return svg(ctx, bars);
}
```

A colour blends in OKLab with straight alpha, exactly as `interpolateColors` blends it: `#ff0000`
to `#0000ff` is `#8c53a2` halfway, not the muddy `#800080` of a channel-by-channel blend, and
`#ffffff` to `#00000000` is `#63636380`, grey and half transparent. While a prop
moves, every frame is drawn anew, so a graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the
length of the action.

## Video inside a graphic: the matte

A graphic cannot read a video's pixels. To show video inside a shape the graphic draws, put the
graphic on the track directly above the video and switch that track to a **matte**: Track ▸ Matte
in the app, or `set_track {track, matte}` over MCP. A matte track's clips are never drawn. What
they show cuts the track directly behind: with `alpha`, the video shows where the graphic is
opaque; with `alpha_inverted`, where it is transparent; with `luma` and `luma_inverted`, by the
brightness of what it draws. `matte: "none"` turns it off. Where the matte track has no clip, the
video shows uncut. The module is written and called exactly as anywhere else. Fill the window in
white so it works in every mode, and animate it as usual: the cut follows each frame.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Window", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { radius: { type: "number", default: 24, min: 0, max: 200 } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const t = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 18 });
  const w = ctx.width * 0.6 * t;
  const h = ctx.height * 0.6 * t;
  return svg(ctx, `<rect x="${(ctx.width - w) / 2}" y="${(ctx.height - h) / 2}"
    width="${w}" height="${h}" rx="${props.radius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`);
}
```

On a matte track a clip's position, scale, opacity, crop and actions still shape the window. Its
blend mode, drop shadow and reflection do nothing. The matted video's own drop shadow follows the
cut-out shape.

## Idioms

### A slide-in

```js
export const meta = { name: "Slide in", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { text: { type: "string", default: "Hello" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const u = ctx.height / 1080;
  const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 18], [-ctx.width / 2, ctx.width / 2],
    { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true });
  return svg(ctx, `<text x="${x}" y="${ctx.height / 2}" text-anchor="middle"
    font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="800" font-size="${120 * u}"
    fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(props.text)}</text>`);
}
```

### A staggered list

```js
export const meta = { name: "Agenda" };
export const schema = {
  items: { type: "string", default: "Intro\nDemo\nQuestions", multiline: true, animate: false },
  accent: { type: "color", default: "#ffcc00" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const u = ctx.height / 1080;
  const rows = props.items.split("\n").filter((s) => s.trim()).map((item, i) => {
    const t = spring({ frame: frame - i * 6, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 16 });
    const y = 300 * u + i * 110 * u;
    return `<g opacity="${Math.min(1, t)}" transform="translate(${(1 - t) * 80 * u} 0)">
      <rect x="${160 * u}" y="${y - 50 * u}" width="${14 * u}" height="${64 * u}" fill="${props.accent}"/>
      <text x="${200 * u}" y="${y}" font-family="'Source Sans 3'" font-weight="600"
        font-size="${64 * u}" fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(item)}</text></g>`;
  });
  return svg(ctx, rows.join(""));
}
```

### A counter

```js
export const meta = { name: "Counter", durationInFrames: 120 };
export const schema = {
  to: { type: "number", default: 25000, min: 0 },
  suffix: { type: "string", default: " views" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const value = interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, props.to], { easing: Easing.outExpo, clamp: true });
  const text = formatNumber(Math.round(value)) + props.suffix;
  return svg(ctx, `<text x="${ctx.width / 2}" y="${ctx.height / 2}" text-anchor="middle"
    font-family="'IBM Plex Mono'" font-weight="500" font-size="${ctx.height / 8}"
    fill="#ffffff">${escapeXml(text)}</text>`);
}
```

### Fit and wrap a title

```js
export const meta = { name: "Title card" };
export const schema = {
  title: { type: "string", default: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" },
};

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const maxWidth = ctx.width * 0.8;
  const base = { family: "Bebas Neue", weight: 400 };
  const size = fitText(props.title, maxWidth * 2, base, { min: 48, max: 220 });
  const font = Object.assign({}, base, { size });
  const lines = wrapText(props.title, maxWidth, font);
  const top = ctx.height / 2 - (lines.length - 1) * size * 0.6;
  const fade = interpolate(frame, [0, 12], [0, 1], { clamp: true });
  return svg(ctx, `<g opacity="${fade}">${textLines(lines,
    { x: ctx.width / 2, y: top, anchor: "middle", fill: "#ffffff", font })}</g>`,
    { background: "#16161a" });
}
```

### A draw-on stroke

`evolvePath` measures the path and answers the dash that draws it up to a
progress of 0–1.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Underline", durationInFrames: 60 };
export const schema = { color: { type: "color", default: "#ff5a36" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const y = ctx.height * 0.62;
  const d = `M ${ctx.width * 0.2} ${y} q ${ctx.width * 0.3} ${ctx.height * 0.05} ${ctx.width * 0.6} 0`;
  const drawn = interpolate(frame, [0, 24], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutCubic, clamp: true });
  const dash = evolvePath(drawn, d);
  return svg(ctx, `<path d="${d}" stroke="${props.color}"
    stroke-width="${ctx.height / 90}" stroke-linecap="round" fill="none"
    stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>`);
}
```

### Follow a path

`getPointAtLength` answers where the path is and which way it is heading;
`rotate(angle)` turns an arrowhead drawn pointing right to match.

```js
export const meta = { name: "Arrow", durationInFrames: 60 };
export const schema = { color: { type: "color", default: "#ffffff" } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const w = ctx.width;
  const h = ctx.height;
  const d = `M ${w * 0.2} ${h * 0.7} C ${w * 0.4} ${h * 0.2} ${w * 0.6} ${h * 0.2} ${w * 0.8} ${h * 0.5}`;
  const drawn = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutCubic, clamp: true });
  const dash = evolvePath(drawn, d);
  const tip = getPointAtLength(d, getLength(d) * drawn);
  const s = h / 36;
  return svg(ctx, `<path d="${d}" stroke="${props.color}" stroke-width="${h / 120}" fill="none"
    stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
    <path d="M ${-s} ${-s * 0.6} L ${s * 0.5} 0 L ${-s} ${s * 0.6} Z" fill="${props.color}"
    transform="translate(${tip.x} ${tip.y}) rotate(${tip.angle})"/>`);
}
```
