tools.name: mcp__framejob__export
tools.description: Starts writing the timeline to a file and answers AT ONCE with {export_id, path, status} — ⌘E, the export sheet's six controls (format, size, frame rate, quality, loudness, range) in the sheet's own vocabulary, all but the frame rate — this exports at the document's rate, or on gif and apng at the format's own rate (12.5 and 25 fps). The export is a job in the Export Queue, run one at a time behind any other export already there; status is queued or running. Follow it with export_status, which never waits — call it again after a pause until status is done, failed or cancelled — and stop it with cancel_export. The export_id lasts until Frame Job quits. Every refusal comes back from this call, before anything is queued: a bad argument, a missing folder, and a graphic clip whose module does not compile; a failure while writing comes back from export_status, failed with its reason (a graphic that fails during the export stops it with no file left, naming the graphic and the frame). The preset is the ENCODING only and the size a separate choice defaulting to the document's own, or on gif and apng to the format's cap; the core resolves both into concrete settings (container, codec, size, rate, range) and hands them to the same exporter the sheet uses, so an agent export and a menu export cannot disagree. An existing file at the path is replaced, and the container's extension is added when the path has none. In an HLG project (set_canvas output) hevc_10bit, prores_422 and prores_4444 write HLG unless dynamic_range says pq or sdr, and every other video preset writes the project's SDR version. What the finished file holds is export_status's done answer.

audio_bitrate.description: Target AAC rate in BITS per second (192000 is 192 kbps) — the sheet's Quality popup. Omit for 192 kbps. Ignored where the sound is not AAC: ProRes, WAV and AIFF all write LPCM, whose rate is its sample format.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

dynamic_range.description: An HDR (HLG) project's picture on hevc_10bit, prores_422 and prores_4444 — the sheet's Dynamic Range popup: hlg (the default; BT.2100 HLG, no Dolby Vision), pq (HDR10: BT.2100 PQ at 1,000 cd/m2, mastering display P3-D65 0.005–1,000 cd/m2, MaxCLL 1,000, MaxFALL 0) or sdr (the SDR version). Every other video preset writes the SDR version; hlg and pq are refused there and in an SDR project, where sdr changes nothing.

loudness_lufs.description: Normalise the whole mix to this integrated loudness, in LUFS — the sheet's Loudness popup, whose rows are -14 (streaming), -16 (podcast) and -23 (EBU R 128 broadcast). The export measures itself first and then applies ONE gain to everything, so relative levels inside the timeline are untouched and no limiter is involved. Omit not to normalise: the export still measures and still reports. Ignored where there is no sound to measure (gif, apng).

path.description: Where to write, e.g. ~/Movies/cut.mp4. The folder must exist.

peak_dbtp.description: The true-peak ceiling that gain is capped against, in dBTP. The sheet fixes it at -1 and this is the knob for anything else. Because normalisation is gain-only, a ceiling with no loudness_lufs beside it would have nothing to cap and is REFUSED rather than accepted and left inert. When the ceiling bites, the file lands quieter than the target asked for and the result's capped_by_peak says so.

preset.description: Export preset id — one per encoding, a container and a codec with no size of its own (that is size's). h264 is what the export sheet opens on. Three rows keep a transparent canvas transparent: prores_4444 and hevc_alpha (the movie rows — see size, which constrains them) and apng. gif is not one of them: it can show a transparent pixel but has no alpha channel, so nothing partial survives it. prores_422, prores_4444 and hevc_10bit keep the compositor's 16-bit frames at 10 bits (ProRes 4444 at 12); h264, hevc and hevc_alpha are 8-bit. Pass a wrong one once and the error lists them all.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

range.description: What to write: the whole timeline (default), or just the in/out range set_range set — the sheet's Range popup.

size.description: Output size — the sheet's Size popup. A row id: document (the default, the document's own size, evened on the formats that need it), 1080p, 720p, 1440p or 2160p (the number is the SHORT edge and the long edge follows the document's aspect, rounded to even, so a vertical project's 1080p is 1080 × 1920), or preset for an image format's cap (gif and apng, where it is the default) — or an explicit [width, height] in px, the sheet's Custom.... Every row exists on every document — a 1920 × 1080 project's 1080p is its own size and is listed anyway — so an id means the same thing wherever it is sent; only preset is confined to gif and apng. Omit for the document size or the image format's cap; a wrong id's error lists the ids. A movie is written at exactly the size asked for, letterboxed if the shape differs by more than a pixel (within a pixel the picture fills the frame instead) — except on prores_4444 and hevc_alpha, where a size of a DIFFERENT SHAPE from the canvas is refused rather than written, because the padding destroys the alpha channel those rows are chosen for; every row id is already the document's own shape, so this only bites on a [width, height] of another shape. h264, hevc, hevc_alpha, hevc_10bit and prores_422 need even dimensions: an odd width or height — the document size on a canvas with an odd edge, or an odd [width, height] — is written one pixel smaller on that edge, and the width and height reported back are the file's. The shape is judged on that even frame: a [width, height] in the canvas's own proportions is never refused for being odd, at any scale; one of another shape is judged as the even size it becomes, which is the size hevc_alpha's refusal names. prores_4444, gif and apng keep an odd edge. On gif and apng a size — the cap, a row, or [width, height] — is a box the picture is fitted inside, aspect kept and never upscaled, and the width and height reported back are the file's: a vertical 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

video_bitrate.description: Target video rate in BITS per second (8000000 is 8 Mbps) — the sheet's Quality popup. Omit to let the preset's own encoder settings decide. Ignored by presets that carry no rate of their own: ProRes is fixed by its profile, and GIF and APNG have no bitrate at all.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__export_status
tools.description: How an export this launch started is going — Window ▸ Export Queue's row for it, read now: it never waits, so call it again after a pause. Always export_id, status (queued, running, done, failed or cancelled), path and elapsed (seconds since export was called, or to the finish once it has finished). running adds progress (0 to 1) and phase while the exporter names one (the loudness measurement). done adds what the file holds: ok, bytes, the settings that were used (preset, container, codec, width, height, fps [num, den], start, duration), burn_in_timecode, dynamic_range in an HLG project (the picture written), loudness for every format that carries sound, normalised or not — summary, integrated_lufs, true_peak_dbtp, sample_peak_dbfs, gain_db, ceiling_dbtp, capped_by_peak and target_lufs when one was asked, read off the mix that was written — and graphic_warnings [{name, frame, message}], each distinct warning a graphic gave while the file was drawn, absent when none. failed and cancelled add reason, the queue row's sentence. Only ids export returned are known, until Frame Job quits.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_graphic
tools.description: Reads the project's graphics/ folder. With name: that module's source, revision (the SHA-256 of its bytes), path, whether it compiles (ok, meta, schema, diagnostics), the clips drawn by it and kept, the revisions of its kept earlier texts, newest first (restore_graphic takes one). Without: folder, the folder's absolute path — where it WILL be when folder_exists is false; the first write_graphic creates it — and every module with its revision, ok and clips, warnings: what the folder's scan skipped or could not watch, in its own sentences, and history: [{name, kept}] for every name with a kept text, deleted modules included. The folder may also be edited with your own file tools: modules (<name>.js), fonts in fonts/ (.ttf, .otf) and pictures in assets/; the app sees a change within a moment. API.md and API.d.ts there are the reference, written by the app, and history/ is the app's too: the kept texts, which restore_graphic reads.

name.description: The module to read. Omit for the folder.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_project
tools.description: The whole project as JSON: canvas (width, height, fps [num, den], background, fit_new_clips, timecode_frames), media, tracks, clips and markers, with next_id — the schema every op edits. Plus the state that is deliberately NOT in the model and lives only in the app: playhead, selection and the in/out range. Read this first: every other tool names things by the ids it reports, and clip, track, marker and media ids share ONE number space, so an id is unambiguous on its own. tracks[0] is the BACK of the layer stack (the bottom lane of the timeline); times are ticks at 600000 per second. missing_media lists media whose file has moved — relink_media points it at the new one. graphics: every module in the package's graphics/ with its revision, whether it compiles, and the clips drawn by it.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__graphic_reference
tools.description: Answers the whole graphics API — the module's shape, ctx, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, limits and idioms — as Markdown, for an LLM to read once before writing a graphic. Needs no project open; a project, when given, must name an open one. Help ▸ Graphics Reference opens the same file.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_frame
tools.description: Renders one frame of the finished timeline as a picture so you can SEE the result — the verification hook. It goes through the same composition and the same Metal compositor an export does, so this is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it. The image comes back both as an image block and as a file on disk whose path the text names. Use it before and after every edit. It writes a PNG to a temporary file unless path or format says otherwise, so a call that names neither is exactly the call it always was. When a graphic in the frame warned or failed, a sentence before the last names the graphic, its frame and the diagnostic; a failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

format.description: The container to write. Default: the path's own extension when it is one of those (.jpg counts as jpeg), else png — so a call with no path and no format writes a PNG, as it always has. An explicit format WINS and the path's extension is REPLACED rather than appended to, so {path: "shot.jpg", format: "png"} writes shot.png. png and heic keep the canvas's alpha; JPEG has no alpha channel: a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

histogram.description: Also measure the frame's histogram, View ▸ Scopes' Histogram: R′, G′, B′ and Y′ counts per 256 levels. The text says what share of pixels clips high and low by Y′, and <image path>.histogram.json holds the four planes' counts and both percentages. Default false.

max_width.description: Cap the image's width in px, aspect kept and never upscaled. Default: the canvas's own size.

parade.description: Also measure the frame's RGB parade, View ▸ Scopes' Parade: R′, G′ and B′ each binned as the waveform bins Y′. The text says what share of pixels each channel clips high and low, and <image path>.parade.json holds the counts keyed red, green and blue (each 256 arrays by column bin, indexed by level) with each channel's clip marks and clip counts. Default false.

path.description: Where to write the file, e.g. ~/Desktop/shot.png. The folder must exist. Omit for a temporary file; either way the text block's last sentence names the file that was written. This is the same writer File ▸ Save Frame... uses, so a PNG written here and one saved from the menu are byte-identical.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

selection.description: An adjustment clip's id: draw what its video.qualifier selects instead of grading — grey, white fully graded, black untouched, times any matte cutting it, its strength not applied — with every layer in front of it left out; black where the clip is not on the frame. View ▸ Show Selection's picture; the view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Refused unless it names an adjustment clip. Default: none.

t.description: The moment to render, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default: the playhead.

ungraded.description: Render as if no clip were graded — every clip's video.color (Light and Color) neutral, everything else kept: View ▸ Show Ungraded's picture. The view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Default false.

vectorscope.description: Also measure the frame's vectorscope, View ▸ Scopes' Vectorscope: Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral (bin 128). The text says what share of pixels is neutral, and <image path>.vectorscope.json holds the counts (256 arrays by Cr bin, indexed by Cb bin), the six 75 % targets' bins and the skin line's angle. Default false.

waveform.description: Also measure the frame's luma waveform, View ▸ Scopes' Waveform: the text says what share of pixels clips high and low, and <image path>.waveform.json holds the 256 × 256 counts (one array per column bin, indexed by level), the clip marks and both percentages. Default false.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_graphic
tools.description: Renders a module in graphics/ WITHOUT a clip — to look at it before placing it. png (the default) answers a contact sheet: the frames on a grid, each frame number printed under its cell, the cells scaled down (never the gaps or labels) so the sheet fits max_width; plus one sentence per frame that failed (drawn as its error card) or warned, with the engine's location. svg answers one frame's SVG text, its diagnostics and the ctx it was drawn with. ctx is a clip's: the canvas fps, durationInFrames from meta (else 5 s), the size from width/height, else meta, else the canvas. svg takes no path, background or max_width, which are the png sheet's, and writes no file. A frame at or past durationInFrames is drawn, with progress 1, as a longer clip draws it. A png sheet draws at most 134217728 px of frames (frames × width × height); past that the call is refused before any frame is drawn. No inspector control mirrors it: a person looks at the preview well.

background.description: What the png sheet is painted on: transparent (the default), checker, or a hex colour (#rgb, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa). Not with format svg.

format.description: png (default): the contact sheet. svg: one frame's SVG text.

frame.description: One frame to draw. Not with frames.

frames.description: The frames to draw, 1 to 16 of them, in order. Not with frame. Omit both for frame 0.

height.description: Height to draw at, in pixels. Default: meta.height, else the canvas.

max_width.description: The widest the png sheet may be, in pixels. Default 2048; 8192 keeps a 1920-wide graphic's two cells at full size. Not with format svg.

name.description: The module: graphics/<name>.js.

path.description: Where to write the png sheet; its folder must exist. Omit for a temporary file. The reply ends "Written to <path>." Not with format svg.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

props.description: The values to draw with, keyed by the schema's names; a key left out draws with the schema's default.

width.description: Width to draw at, in pixels. Default: meta.width, else the canvas.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__save_project
tools.description: Saves the project. A project that has never been saved — a new_project with no path, or a movie opened as one — needs a path; passing a path always writes there (Save As). Returns once the package is really on disk. A path another open project holds is refused; close_project closes that one first.

path.description: Where to write the .framejob package. Required the first time; otherwise the project is written back to its own file.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_action
tools.description: Moves or re-times an action, or changes its easing curve. Same overlap checks as add_action. Refused when the action would then end past the clip's end and later than it ended before, so an action already running past the clip's end (a trim can leave one there) can still be re-curved, moved earlier or shortened. When the action's end names a speed, the change moves how much source the clip reads, and one that would read past the end of its media is refused, naming the latest clip end that fits. Captions on a Captions track wholly inside a clip with sound are re-timed with it in the same step: captions_retimed lists them, and captions_removed those whose speech it no longer plays.

action.description: Action id (get_project lists each clip's actions).

curve.description: How the values ease from start to end.

duration.description: New length, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

scope.description: Edit INSIDE a nest, by nest id — get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows. With it, every id in this call — clips, tracks, actions — is looked up in THAT nest's own tracks and clips instead of the timeline's, and every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero (a nest has no speed, so the whole mapping is t minus the nest clip's start); media ids are unaffected, because a nest shares the document's media. The op itself is unchanged and one call is still one undo step. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. Eight ops have no meaning inside a nest and refuse by name when you ask for one: add_marker, set_marker, remove_marker, set_canvas, add_media, relink_media, remove_media, add_adjustment_clip. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. The two that carry a TIME — add_marker, and set_marker with a time — are refused instead, because a marker is at project time while the playhead inside a nest is not, so the tick you would send means the wrong frame. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

start.description: New start in CLIP time, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_action_end
tools.description: Sets what an action animates TO. The patch is the action's end state and MERGES into it key by key at every depth (a one-key shadow keeps the rest of it); a key set to null is REMOVED from the end state, so that property stops being animated. Groups are video, audio and text, with the same keys as set_video / set_audio / set_text — a colour is FOUR numbers here too, and it ramps in OKLab with straight alpha, as a graphic colour does; video.chroma.key's three numbers do too. A bad key or value is refused by its path with the group in it (video.filters[1].kind), though values are NOT range-checked: an animation may aim past what a stored property could hold. Two keys are refused: video.motion, a preset anchored to the clip's two ends rather than a value to ramp between (set it with set_video), and text.words, whose times belong to speech. A GRAPHIC clip's props are a fourth group, graphic: {props: {<key>: <value>}}, keyed by its module's schema and checked as set_graphic checks them, min and max included, against the module as graphics/ holds it NOW; the app reads that schema, so never send one. A number and a colour ramp along the curve: a number arrives with decimals (64 to 129 is 96.5 halfway), so a module that needs a whole number rounds it, and a colour blends in OKLab, as interpolateColors does, with straight alpha. A string, a boolean and an enum switch to the end's value when the action ENDS. An image (asset) prop switches to the end's image when the action ENDS; "" names no image there (null removes the prop from the end). A prop its module marks animate: false is refused: set it with set_graphic. A prop the clip holds no value for starts from the module's current default, written into the clip in the same undo step. graphic.props.<key>: null removes that prop from the end, graphic: null the whole group. get_project shows kinds beside props; the app writes it and ignores one you send, so an end read back can be sent again. While the module is missing or does not compile a prop value is refused (needs its module's schema) — get_graphic says why — and a null still removes. speed, a number beside the groups, is a MEDIA clip's rate (×0.1–×1000, clamped): the clip ramps from the rate in force to it along the curve and holds it after; the clip keeps its start and length and plays more or less source, and an end rate that would read past the end of its media is refused, naming the largest end rate that fits. speed: null removes it. Above ×12 the clip's audio is left out, and the answer carries audio_left_out and audio_note. With speed in the patch, captions on a Captions track wholly inside a clip with sound are re-timed with it in the same step: captions_retimed lists them, and captions_removed those whose speech it no longer plays.

action.description: Action id.

off.description: "group.key" paths (video.shadow, text.width) to switch OFF at the end — stored as null, where a null in patch removes. Optional keys only; never graphic.

patch.description: {video?: {...}, audio?: {...}, text?: {...}, graphic?: {props: {...}}, speed?: number} — the properties the animation ends at.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_audio
tools.description: Changes the clips' BASE audio properties — volume, mute, fades, ducking, mono, pitch preservation, pan, compression and noise reduction. Merges like set_video; duck or compressor set to null removes it.

patch.description: Audio properties to merge. Keys: volume (0–4, 1 = unity), muted, fade_in, fade_out (ticks), duck (null or {level, attack, release}), mono, keep_pitch, pan (-1 hard left ... +1 hard right), compressor (null or {threshold_db, ratio, attack, release, makeup_db} — the two times in ticks), noise_reduction (0–1). duck and compressor are OBJECTS and they MERGE: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {duck: null} clears the whole thing.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_canvas
tools.description: Changes the project's canvas — the fixed frame every clip is composited into. rescale_clips multiplies every clip's x, y and scale by the size ratio, which is what keeps a layout looking the same when you resize; without it the clips keep their pixel positions. Changing fps re-snaps every clip start and duration to the new frame grid.

background.description: Colour behind every layer as [r, g, b, a], each 0–1. Four numbers exactly: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped.

fit_new_clips.description: Give a new clip Fit scale when its source is bigger than the canvas.

fps.description: Frame rate as [numerator, denominator]: [30, 1], [30000, 1001] for 29.97, [24000, 1001] for 23.976.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels.

rescale_clips.description: Scale every clip's placement with the canvas (default false).

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_graphic
tools.description: Patches what graphic clips are drawn from: name (another module), width, height, length (the graphic's own timeline in ticks; null ends it with the clip) and props, merged key by key — a null prop removes its key, except a key the module's schema has that an action on the clip animates (set_action_end's graphic): that one is set to the schema's default, so the animation keeps its start. A patch naming props or name is checked against the schema of the module it names, else of the one module every clip is drawn by; clips drawn by two different modules are refused for props. A clip that is not a graphic is an error. These are the BASE props; to animate one, add_action and then set_action_end.

patch.description: The keys to change: name, width, height, length, props.

tools.description: Moves the playhead and seeks the preview. View state, not an edit: nothing is undoable and the project is untouched. split, freeze_frame and add_marker default to this time.

t.description: Time in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_text
tools.description: Changes a text clip's words and typography. Merges like set_video; outline, backdrop and width set to null clear them (a null width restores auto-sizing). Position and scale are set_video's, not this tool's.

patch.description: Text properties to merge. Keys: content, font (a PostScript name), size (px), color, align (left|center|right), valign (top|middle|bottom), line_spacing, tracking, outline (null or {width, color}), backdrop (null or {color, padding, radius}), width (null for auto-sizing, or a wrap width in px), animation (null or {kind: typewriter|word_fade|line_rise, in, out} — how the words arrive and leave. in and out are DURATIONS in ticks measured from the clip's own first and last frame, not times; either may be 0 for no ramp at that end, and in + out longer than the clip simply shows a partial reveal, and both are snapped to the document's frame grid. Like shadow and backdrop it MERGES: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {animation: null} clears the whole thing), case (as_written|upper — applied before layout; it never changes the word count), words (one {start, end} per whitespace token of content, in clip ticks, or [] for an untimed page — a content change that alters the count must send words: [] in the same patch), word_style (null or {mode: highlight|build, active_color, active_scale 1–1.5, active_pill {color, padding, radius, glide}, spoken_color, upcoming_color, active_fill, pause_dim 0–1} — how the word being said is drawn; it replaces animation. Three looks, each off by default: active_pill.glide (true|false) slides the pill from the word before to the active one over 0.2 s, or sooner when the next word starts sooner, instead of jumping; active_fill (true|false) fills the active word left to right from its start to its end, taking 0.6 s at most — the part said in active_color and the rest in upcoming_color, or not yet drawn in build mode; in highlight mode it shows only where those two colours differ; pause_dim fades the words and the pill to 1 − pause_dim of their opacity in a pause of 0.25 s or more — after one word's end until the next one's start, before a late first word, and after the last word until the clip ends — over 0.1 s each way, and outside 0–1 it is refused). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_video
tools.description: Changes the clips' BASE video properties — position, scale, rotation, opacity, crop, corner radius, shadow, colour, chroma key, filters, reflection, spotlight and motion (what the clip does on its way in, on its way out and all the way through). The patch MERGES AT EVERY DEPTH: keys you leave out keep their values, inside a nested object too — a patch of just {shadow: {blur: 20}} keeps the shadow's colour, angle and distance — and shadow, chroma, reflection, spotlight or motion set to null clears it. A LIST is the exception: filters and obscure each replace whole, so send the whole stack and [] to clear it. A key or a value the vocabulary does not have is an error naming its dotted path (array indices included) and the value you sent; nothing is dropped, corrected or clamped. Placement is spec §5.3: the source rectangle is centred at the canvas centre plus (x, y), scaled, then rotated about that centre, and crop removes edges in place without shifting the content. To animate a property instead, add_action and then set_action_end. On an adjustment clip only color, wheels, curves, look, the point filters and opacity (the grade's strength) do anything, the qualifier narrows which pixels they reach, and blur, sharpen, pixelate or a blend mode is an error.

patch.description: Video properties to merge into the clip's base props. Keys: x, y (canvas px from the canvas centre, y DOWN), scale (1 = native pixels, 0.01–10), rotation (degrees, positive turns clockwise on screen), opacity (0–1), crop ({l, t, r, b} in SOURCE px — cropping never shifts the content), corner_radius (source px), shadow (null or {color, opacity, blur, angle, distance}), color ({brightness, contrast, saturation, hue, exposure, temperature, tint, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, vibrance, fade}, each 0 = unchanged and any subset merging — exposure is -3 to 3 (EV), fade 0–1 and the other seven tone keys -1 to 1, refused outside; a positive temperature is warmer, a positive tint more magenta; hue is in degrees, and a positive hue turns every colour's HSV hue that far, red → yellow → green, keeping its Rec. 709 luma), chroma (null or {key: [r, g, b], tolerance, softness, spill}), filters (an ARRAY of {kind, amount} applied in order, at most 4 — kind is blur|sharpen|pixelate|sepia|noir|vignette|invert and amount is 0–1; send the whole array, since it replaces rather than merges, and [] clears the stack), reflection (null or {opacity, height, gap, falloff} — height and falloff are fractions of the layer's cropped height, gap is source px), spotlight (null or {shape: rect|ellipse, x, y, width, height, feather, dim, zoom} — the centre and the box are SOURCE px from the cropped rect's centre, dim is how much darker it is OUTSIDE and zoom 1–2 magnifies what is inside), obscure (an ARRAY of {shape: rect|ellipse, x, y, width, height, feather, kind, amount} that HIDES what is under each one, at most 4 — kind is blur|pixelate and amount is 0–1, feather is the source px the effect ramps in over, and the centre and the box are SOURCE px from the cropped rect's centre, the same frame the spotlight uses. Like filters it is replaced whole rather than merged, so send the whole array and [] to clear it), blend (how this layer combines with what is already on the canvas: normal|multiply|screen|add|overlay|darken|lighten|difference — normal is source-over, which is what every project drew before this key existed. A blend needs something UNDER it: over the empty canvas multiply, darken and overlay read black while screen, add, lighten and difference change nothing, so add_background is usually the call before this one. It is forced to normal for the length of a cross dissolve, whose own weighting requires it, so what the frame shows there can legitimately differ from the value get_project reports), motion (what the clip DOES: null, or {in, out, during} — in and out are {kind: fade|zoom_in|zoom_out|slide_left|slide_right|slide_up|slide_down|spin|pop, duration: ticks} measured from the clip's first and last frame, during is {kind: pulse|shake|spin|bounce|drift, amount: 0–1, period: ticks} over the whole clip and drift ignores its period. Like every other object here it MERGES: a slot you leave out keeps what is stored, a slot set to null clears that slot, {motion: null} clears the whole preset, and a motion with no slot left reads back as null. The two durations are snapped to the document's frame grid and the period is snapped with a floor of ONE frame (it divides in every during formula and has no zero), so get_project can answer with a tick count near the one you sent rather than the one itself. in + out longer than the clip scales both down to meet rather than refusing. It is NOT an animation target — set_action_end refuses it — and get_project reports the clip UN-MOVED, since the preset becomes placement only when a frame is rendered), wheels ({lift, gamma, gain}, each {x, y, master}, each -1 to 1 and 0 = unchanged: x, y is the colour push, its angle the hue (0° red, 120° green, 240° blue) and its length the strength, and must lie inside the unit circle (x2 + y2 ≤ 1); master is the brightness; refused outside, never clamped. Any subset MERGES, so {wheels: {lift: {x: 0.2, y: -0.1}}} keeps lift's master and the other two wheels. Applied after color's tone and before look: lift moves black and holds white, gain moves white and holds black, gamma moves the middle and holds both ends), curves ({master, red, green, blue}, each a list of 2 to 16 [x, y] points, x strictly rising, x and y 0–1 inclusive; refused outside, never clamped. A list REPLACES that channel whole, null removes it, and a curve with every y = x from x 0 to x 1 is the identity, stored as no curve. Each channel is a monotone spline (Fritsch–Carlson) through its points, flat outside its first and last x; a colour is red(master(v)). Applied after wheels and before look. In an action's end an identity curve animates to neutral (an identity on either side takes the other curve's x's); two curves of different point counts blend their values across the action. Two hue curves too, hue_hue (Hue vs Hue) and hue_sat (Hue vs Sat): each 2 to 16 [hue, value] points, hue in degrees 0 ≤ hue < 360 strictly rising; hue_hue's value is a shift in degrees -180–180 (0 none) and hue_sat's a saturation gain 0–2 (1 none); a curve whose every value is its none is the identity, stored as no curve. Each is a periodic spline that wraps at 0/360. Applied after the channel curves and before look, at the colour's HSV hue read once: a positive shift turns HSV hue red → yellow → green keeping Rec. 709 luma, the gain scales saturation about that luma; a grey or near-grey (chroma at most 0.02) is left alone, and the effect fades in up to chroma 0.06), qualifier (adjustment clips only — anything else is an error naming the clip; which pixels the clip's grade reaches, read from the picture behind it BEFORE the grade: {hue: {center, width, softness}, saturation: {low, high, softness}, luma: {low, high, softness}, invert, blur}. hue is in degrees: center 0–360 (wraps), width 0–360 fully selected about the centre, softness 0–180 of fall-off outside each edge; a colour with chroma under about 0.06 has no hue and is never selected by it. saturation is HSV saturation (chroma / max, and near-black reads as 0) and luma Rec. 709 Y′, each low ≤ high and softness 0–1. A range MERGES: {hue: {}} turns hue on at {30, 50, 25} (saturation and luma at {0, 1, 0.1}), a partial range keeps the rest, null turns it off; the weight is the product of the ranges on, inverted by invert: true. blur 0–1 (0 off) softens that weight by a Gaussian of 24·blur canvas pixels, never the matte; it draws nothing with no range on. Refused outside the bounds, never clamped. In an action the numbers animate, the hue centre the short way round (350 to 10 passes 0); a range turned on or off and invert switch at the end. render_frame {selection: clip} shows what it selects), look (null, or {kind: warm|cool|teal_orange|vivid|faded|vintage|dramatic|black_white|lut, media, amount: 0–1} — one of the eight built-in looks, or lut: an imported .cube file, media its media id (import_media imports one), required with lut and refused with any other kind; applied after color and before the filters; amount is how much of it, 1 when left out, refused outside 0–1. It MERGES: a new kind keeps the clip's amount, a built-in kind replaces a LUT, an amount alone needs a clip that already has a look, and {look: null} removes it. In an action's end the amount animates and a change of kind or of LUT switches at the end). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped. chroma's key is the one exception, three numbers with no alpha.

content.text: <total_tokens>14993987 tokens left</total_tokens>

Mostly yes. The steps are already in the frame Frame Job renders, before the H.264 encode touches it.

**What I measured** on the intro's green glow, along an 800 px line from the left edge to the logo:

| | Green levels used | Typical flat band | Widest band |
|---|---|---|---|
| `render_frame` output (before encoding) | 43 (values 23–65) | 14 px | 50 px |
| Exported H.264, same frame | 41 | 10 px | 56 px |

The glow only moves from #0D1512 to a mid green, so it spans about 40 code values per channel. Spread over 800 px, each value becomes a flat ring about 15–50 px wide. Every edge you see is a single-step change, which is exactly what 8-bit can't subdivide. Red, green and blue step at different radii, so the rings also pick up a faint colour tint.

**Why it's 8-bit.** Graphic clips are rasterized by resvg into 8-bit BGRA. That's a recorded decision (spec §11 PR-5: graphics, text and shapes stay 8-bit) even though the compositor itself works in 16-bit float. So a 10-bit export (HEVC 10-bit or ProRes) would not fix it: the steps are baked in before the compositor sees the graphic. The H.264 encode then adds a little on top, making bands slightly narrower and blockier, but it isn't the main cause.

**What would fix it**
1. **Add grain in the graphics (works today).** A faint noise layer over each gradient, using an SVG `feTurbulence` filter at about 3–5% opacity, breaks the hard band edges into texture even at 8-bit. It's the standard cure for banding in motion design. It does cost bitrate, so I'd also export at around 20–25 Mbps so H.264 keeps the grain instead of smoothing it back into bands. Only the intro, outro and colour-field scenes have large soft gradients.
2. **Make the gradient span less dark range.** A smaller, brighter glow uses fewer, more spread-out steps in a range where the eye notices them less. This is a design compromise, not a real fix.
3. **Fix it in the product.** Graphics would need either a deeper raster or dithering when the gradient is drawn. Either one goes against the PR-5 decision, so it's your call. I can file an issue for it.

Want me to do option 1 on those three scenes and re-export?

lastPrompt: I don't want to fix just this video. It's very obvious with every video. Can we expand the bit range of svg?

content.text:
Yes, but expanding the SVG depth alone won't remove the banding from most videos. There are two 8-bit steps, and the second applies to every H.264 export.

**1. The graphic raster is 8-bit.** Graphics are drawn by resvg on top of tiny-skia 0.12, and tiny-skia only has an RGBA8 pixel buffer. It already computes gradients in 32-bit float internally, then rounds to 8 bits when it writes the pixel. To keep that precision we would have to:
- patch tiny-skia, vendored, to write 16-bit pixels;
- force every graphic through its float pipeline. Today simple fills take a faster 8-bit path, so drawing a graphic would get slower; a spike would measure by how much;
- accept that resvg's own filters (blur, `feTurbulence`) would stay 8-bit unless patched too.

On the app side the graphic texture becomes `rgba16Float`, which the compositor already uses. Each cached graphic frame doubles in memory, so the graphics cache (a quarter of RAM) holds half as many frames. This reopens spec §11 PR-5, which deliberately kept graphics 8-bit.

**2. The final 8-bit output has no dithering.** The compositor works in 16-bit float, but H.264 and 8-bit HEVC (the default and most common exports) round it to 8 bits, and I found no dither anywhere in the app or shaders. Even a perfect 16-bit gradient lands back in 8-bit steps at that point. The same is true of graded deep footage, such as a smooth sky. Only the 10-bit and ProRes exports would show the benefit of deeper graphics.

**What I'd build**
- **Deep graphics:** tiny-skia patched to write 16-bit, uploaded as `rgba16Float`. This fixes banding in 10-bit and ProRes deliverables and stops gradients losing levels when a graphic is graded, faded or scaled.
- **Dither at every 8-bit output:** a small deterministic noise, about half a level, added in the compositor when the target is 8-bit (H.264, HEVC 8-bit, PNG stills). This is what makes the bands disappear in an ordinary H.264 file, and it helps video as well as graphics.

The dither alone would fix most of what you're seeing for most deliverables, and it's the smaller change. Deep graphics without the dither would barely change an H.264 export.

**How I'd run it:** a short spike first, then the road map in a worktree lane, recording the new §11 decision (superseding PR-5 for graphics) before any code. The spike would answer three things on the intro gradient:
- how many levels the patched raster keeps;
- how much slower drawing and how much more memory it costs;
- whether the dithered H.264 export still shows bands at default bitrate.

Should I start with the spike?

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kevingalligan-devel-framejob/8f8ab556-be01-4c5e-8a57-e4a4085a4571/scratchpad/deep-graphics-issue.md <<'EOF'
Graphic clips are rasterized at 8 bits per channel (spec §11 PR-5), so a smooth gradient drawn by a graphic module loses its levels before the 16-bit-float compositor ever sees it. The owner wants the bit range of SVG rasters expanded; output dithering (the 8-bit exports) is being done first as a separate change, and this issue holds the deeper part.

## What was measured (2026-10-27)

The promo's intro graphic draws a radial gradient from `#0D1512` to a mid green over ~800 px. Along row 540, x 0–800, of a 1920×1080 `render_frame` PNG:

- green spans code values 23–65: 43 distinct levels, 51 steps, every step exactly one level;
- median flat run 14 px, widest 50 px: visible concentric rings, faintly tinted because R, G and B step at different radii.

The same frame decoded from the H.264 export keeps 41 levels (median run 10 px, widest 56 px): the encode is not the main cause. The steps are in the raster.

## Why it is 8-bit

- `graphic/` renders through resvg 0.48.1 on tiny-skia 0.12.0. tiny-skia's only `Pixmap` is RGBA8.
- Its highp pipeline already evaluates gradients in f32, and rounds to u8 at the store stage. Its lowp pipeline (u16 fixed point) runs whenever every stage has a lowp form, as simple fills do. It has no dithering (a `// TODO` about `dither_rate` in `pipeline/blitter.rs`).
- resvg's filters (`feGaussianBlur`, `feTurbulence`, …) operate on 8-bit buffers.

## What expanding it would take

1. A vendored tiny-skia patch: a 16-bit (f16 or u16) `Pixmap`, a deep store stage for highp, and forcing highp for graphics. Raster time will rise; measure it.
2. resvg's filters: patch them to the deep buffer, or document that a filtered region stays 8-bit.
3. App side: the graphic texture becomes `rgba16Float` (the compositor is already 16F, PR-1). The graphic raster cache (G-37, RAM/4 budget) holds half as many frames per byte; re-measure the budget and the prefetch (G-36).
4. A new spec §11 decision superseding PR-5 for graphics (text clips, shapes, stills and captions are PR-5's other 8-bit members; say which follow).
5. Proofs: graphics_proof and every frozen graphic baseline compare 8-bit pixels; they re-record or gain a deep comparison.

Payoff: banding-free graphics in the 10-bit and ProRes deliverables, and gradients that keep their levels when a graphic is graded, faded or scaled. For 8-bit exports the output dither (done separately) is what removes the bands, so do this after it.
EOF

## What was measured (2026-10-27)

The promo's intro graphic draws a radial gradient from `#0D1512` to a mid green over ~800 px. Along row 540, x 0–800, of a 1920×1080 `render_frame` PNG:

- green spans code values 23–65: 43 distinct levels, 51 steps, every step exactly one level;
- median flat run 14 px, widest 50 px: visible concentric rings, faintly tinted because R, G and B step at different radii.

The same frame decoded from the H.264 export keeps 41 levels (median run 10 px, widest 56 px): the encode is not the main cause. The steps are in the raster.

## Why it is 8-bit

- `graphic/` renders through resvg 0.48.1 on tiny-skia 0.12.0. tiny-skia's only `Pixmap` is RGBA8.
- Its highp pipeline already evaluates gradients in f32, and rounds to u8 at the store stage. Its lowp pipeline (u16 fixed point) runs whenever every stage has a lowp form, as simple fills do. It has no dithering (a `// TODO` about `dither_rate` in `pipeline/blitter.rs`).
- resvg's filters (`feGaussianBlur`, `feTurbulence`, …) operate on 8-bit buffers.

## What expanding it would take

1. A vendored tiny-skia patch: a 16-bit (f16 or u16) `Pixmap`, a deep store stage for highp, and forcing highp for graphics. Raster time will rise; measure it.
2. resvg's filters: patch them to the deep buffer, or document that a filtered region stays 8-bit.
3. App side: the graphic texture becomes `rgba16Float` (the compositor is already 16F, PR-1). The graphic raster cache (G-37, RAM/4 budget) holds half as many frames per byte; re-measure the budget and the prefetch (G-36).
4. A new spec §11 decision superseding PR-5 for graphics (text clips, shapes, stills and captions are PR-5's other 8-bit members; say which follow).
5. Proofs: graphics_proof and every frozen graphic baseline compare 8-bit pixels; they re-record or gain a deep comparison.

Payoff: banding-free graphics in the 10-bit and ProRes deliverables, and gradients that keep their levels when a graphic is graded, faded or scaled. For 8-bit exports the output dither (done separately) is what removes the bands, so do this after it.
EOF

Dithering is underway but nothing is built yet. Triage judged it a full change, touching the shader, the compositor's 8-bit outputs, a new spec decision and a proof, so the design stage is running in the background in `~/devel/framejob-dither`.

**Filed for later:**
- **#374** (deep graphic rasters, in the Post Release project) holds today's measurements and the work list:
  - a patched tiny-skia that can write 16-bit pixels;
  - resvg's filters;
  - 16-bit-float graphic textures, which halve how many frames the graphics cache holds;
  - re-recorded proof baselines;
  - a new spec decision replacing PR-5.

**Doing now:**
- **#375** (dither):
  - About ±½ level of deterministic dither wherever the compositor's output is written at 8 bits: H.264 and 8-bit HEVC exports, 8-bit stills from `render_frame` and Save Frame, and the preview if it shows 8-bit.
  - Always on, with no setting.
  - Never on 10/12-bit outputs or alpha.
  - Colours that sit exactly on an 8-bit level stay byte-identical.
- **How it runs:** design → adversarial review → implement → review, ending with `make gate` and a commit fast-forwarded onto main. Nothing gets pushed.

**One limit:** because graphics stay 8-bit until #374, the dither can't add levels inside a graphic's own gradient. It dithers everything computed in float on top: opacity, fades, dissolves, grading, scaling and deep-decoded video. The proof will measure the bands before and after on the promo-style dark gradient, in a still and in a decoded H.264 export, so we'll see how much it helps that case. If the design hits a choice you should make, such as visible grain or file size against band removal, it will stop and I'll bring it to you.

Frame Job is a native video editor for macOS (Apple Silicon, macOS 26). This 90-second tour covers the major features, with a focus on motion graphics: graphic clips drawn every frame by a small JavaScript module, with their properties as inspector controls and animatable from the timeline.

0:00 Intro & editing
0:13 Motion graphics: code, built-ins, timeline actions, matte tracks
0:45 Colour grading & captions
0:58 Audio clean-up, screen & camera recording, export

What's in it:
• Editing — layered tracks, trim, slip, roll, split, ripple delete, nests
• Motion graphics — write a module in JavaScript or start from six built-ins (Bar Chart, Callout, Counter, Kinetic Type, Lower Third, Title Card); animate any property with actions; put footage inside any shape with matte tracks
• Colour — wheels, curves, looks and .cube LUTs, qualifiers, scopes, HDR and camera log
• Captions — transcribed on your Mac or with AssemblyAI, as subtitles or word-by-word
• Clean-up — Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words in one undo step; Synchronize Audio; speed ramps
• Recording — a display or window, system audio and mic, with your camera in the corner
• Export — H.264, HEVC, ProRes, HDR10/HLG, GIF and more, from a queue that runs while you edit
• AI on your own key — the built-in Assistant, or any MCP client such as Claude Code driving the whole editor

This video was made by Claude, using Frame Job's MCP tools.

Download: https://github.com/kpgalligan/framejob/releases/latest/download/FrameJob.dmg
Source: https://github.com/kpgalligan/framejob

Music: "Electronic Corporate" by Orvien

**Open Video…** in the Welcome window — creates an *untitled* project sized and
rated to that file, with the file as the first clip on Track 1, ready to cut. A
portrait phone clip opens portrait, and a 29.97 fps file stays 29.97. **Save**
then writes a `.framejob` package, offered next to the source.

## Features

**Projects and media.** Movies, sound and pictures from everything macOS plays,
plus WebM and MKV copied in without re-encoding; missing files relinked;
Consolidate Media copies footage into the package.
→ [Projects and media](docs/guide/projects-and-media.md)

**Timeline.** One kind of track that holds any clip; a frame-accurate ruler,
filmstrips and waveforms, zoom about the cursor, snapping, markers, an in/out
range, track mute, solo and lock, clip names and colour labels.
→ [The timeline and playback](docs/guide/timeline.md)

**Editing.** Move, nudge, trim, slip, roll, split, lift, ripple delete, close
gap, insert time, insert and overwrite, copy and paste, Paste Attributes, and
nests that group clips into one.
→ [Editing clips](docs/guide/editing.md)

**Canvas and layers.** Move, scale, rotate and crop on the preview; opacity,
blend modes, shadows, filters, chroma key, spotlight and obscure; text, shape,
image and background clips; matte tracks that cut the track behind them.
→ [Canvas, layers, text and shapes](docs/guide/canvas-and-layers.md)

**Motion and transitions.** Actions that ease any property to a new state over
a span — Zoom to Region for screencasts — motion presets for entrances, exits
and continuous movement, and thirteen transition styles.
→ [Motion, actions and transitions](docs/guide/motion-and-transitions.md)

**Speed.** Constant speed or fit to a length, ⌥-drag rate stretch, keep pitch,
reverse, freeze frame, and speed ramps — **Clip ▸ Speed Ramp…** makes a Ramp
Up, Ramp Down, Speed Dip or Speed Burst in one step.
→ [Speed, reverse and freeze frames](docs/guide/speed.md)

**Audio.** Per-clip volume, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan and
mono; Normalize; Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by
their sound, drift included.
→ [Audio](docs/guide/audio.md)

**Clean-up tools.** Remove Silences cuts dead air by voice or by level; Remove
Filler Words cuts the ums and uhs on their own timings. Both preview the cuts
and make them as one undo step.
→ [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md)

**Captions.** Import SubRip, export SubRip or WebVTT; generate captions on this Mac
or with AssemblyAI, as two-line subtitles or word-by-word captions in five
styles. Every caption is an ordinary text clip.
→ [Captions and transcription](docs/guide/captions.md)

**Colour grading.** Light and colour controls, three wheels, curves, eight
built-in looks and your own `.cube` LUTs, adjustment clips with qualifiers,
Show Ungraded, and waveform, parade, vectorscope and histogram scopes.
→ [Colour grading](docs/guide/color-grading.md)

**HDR and colour management.** iPhone HDR, HDR10, wide gamut and camera log
read as what they are; SDR or HDR (HLG) projects; HLG, HDR10 and SDR-version
deliverables, with Show SDR Version to preview the last.
→ [HDR and colour management](docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md)

**Motion graphics.** Graphic clips drawn every frame by a small JavaScript
module: six built-ins (Bar Chart, Callout, Counter, Kinetic Type, Lower Third,
Title Card), properties as inspector controls, your own modules too.
→ [Motion graphics](docs/guide/graphics.md)

**Screen recording.** A display or a window, with system audio, microphone and
click rings, at 30 or 60 fps, into a new project or at the playhead; a camera,
on its own or beside the screen as a corner talking head; or a
microphone-only voice-over.
→ [Screen recording](docs/guide/screen-recording.md)

**Export.** H.264, HEVC (8-bit, 10-bit, with alpha), ProRes 422 and 4444,
M4A, WAV, AIFF, GIF and animated PNG; loudness targets, presets, an Export
Queue that runs while you edit, and single frames as stills.
→ [Exporting](docs/guide/export.md)

**The Assistant.** A conversation with Claude in the inspector that edits the
open project with the same tools an agent uses, asks before it writes a file,
and shows what each turn cost.
→ [The Assistant](docs/guide/assistant.md)

**Agents over MCP.** The whole editor as MCP tools — one per edit plus open,
save, render a frame, export and the rest — for Claude Code or any MCP client.
→ [Driving Frame Job from an AI agent](docs/guide/mcp.md)

Also: [Settings](docs/guide/settings.md) and
[Menus and keyboard shortcuts](docs/guide/menus-and-shortcuts.md).

## Getting Frame Job

The newest signed and notarized build is always at
<https://github.com/kpgalligan/framejob/releases/latest/download/FrameJob.dmg>.
While the repository is private, the link works only for people with access to
it. Open the DMG and drag Frame Job to Applications. An installed copy
updates itself (Frame Job ▸ Check for Updates…, [Settings](docs/guide/settings.md#updates)).

To build it yourself, see [Developing Frame Job](docs/developing.md).

## Using it with an AI agent

Frame Job serves its editor as MCP tools on a local socket only programs you
run can open. An MCP client reaches it through `framejob-mcp`, a helper inside
the app, which starts Frame Job in the background on the first tool call if it
is not running. **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ MCP ▸ Copy MCP Command** puts the
Claude Code registration line on the clipboard, with your copy's path:

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user framejob -- '/Applications/Frame Job.app/Contents/Helpers/framejob-mcp'
```

[MCP](docs/guide/mcp.md) covers other clients and every tool;
[the Assistant](docs/guide/assistant.md) is the same tools inside the window.

## Documentation

- [The user guide](docs/guide/README.md) — every feature, by task.
- [The graphics API](docs/graphics-api.md) — writing a graphic module.
- [Manual checks](docs/manual-checks.md) — what only a person at the machine
  can confirm, run before each release.
- [The spec](designs/spec/README.md) — the normative design, one file per
  section.
- [Developing Frame Job](docs/developing.md) — building, testing, the
  architecture and publishing a release.

## Building

Xcode 26, Rust, xcodegen and bun; then `make app`. Everything else is in
[docs/developing.md](docs/developing.md).

questions.question: The dither design confirms that output dither won't change a plain, opaque SVG gradient at all. Every pixel resvg writes already sits exactly on an 8-bit level, so there's nothing between levels to dither. That's the case you're seeing. It only helps where the compositor creates in-between values: opacity, fades, dissolves, grading, scaling and deep video. To fix the SVG gradients themselves, the dither has to happen where tiny-skia rounds each gradient to 8 bits: a small vendored patch adding a dither stage to its gradient pipeline, the same thing Skia proper does. That's far less than #374's 16-bit rasters, and it removes the bands in every output. How should I proceed?

options.description: Add the gradient dither to the vendored tiny-skia as part of #375, then the output dither. It fixes the SVG gradients you're seeing in every export, plus the bands from fades, grading and video. Graphic proof baselines that contain gradients are re-recorded.

options.label: Output dither only
options.description: Keep #375 as designed. It fixes bands from opacity, fades, dissolves, grading, scaling and deep video, but opaque SVG gradients keep their bands until #374 or a later change.

options.label: Raster dither only
options.description: Only patch tiny-skia's gradients. It fixes the SVG case, but leaves fades, grading and video quantized as they are now.

Every pixel resvg writes already sits exactly on an 8-bit level, so there's nothing between levels to dither. That's the case you're seeing. It only helps where the compositor creates in-between values: opacity, fades, dissolves, grading, scaling and deep video. To fix the SVG gradients themselves, the dither has to happen where tiny-skia rounds each gradient to 8 bits: a small vendored patch adding a dither stage to its gradient pipeline, the same thing Skia proper does. That's far less than #374's 16-bit rasters, and it removes the bands in every output. How should I proceed?"="Both, raster first (Recommended)". You can now continue with these answers in mind.

H=~/.claude/litecode/framejob/dither-375; cat > $H/01a-owner-answer.md <<'EOF'
# Owner answer, 2026-10-27

Question put: the output dither (01-spec) leaves an opaque, unscaled SVG gradient byte-identical. That is the owner's visible complaint. Options were: both, with the raster first; output only; raster only.

Answer: **"Both, raster first."** A dither stage goes into tiny-skia's gradient pipeline, the point where a gradient is rounded to 8 bits, as a vendored patch. That runs FIRST, as its own litecode run (`~/.claude/litecode/framejob/dither-375-raster/`), merged to main before this run continues.

When this run resumes, the final design (03) answers 02-objections.md AND re-reads the merged raster dither:
- F2 ("an opaque gradient is unchanged") becomes the raster run's territory;
- the §11 entry numbering follows whatever the raster run recorded.
EOF
R=~/.claude/litecode/framejob/dither-375-raster; mkdir -p $R && { cat <<'EOF'
# Request — #375 part 1: dither graphic gradients where tiny-skia rounds them to 8 bits

Owner, 2026-10-27. Dark SVG gradients in graphic clips show obvious bands in every video. The measurement is in #374: a radial `#0D1512` → mid-green gradient over about 800 px uses 43 green levels, in single-level steps 14–50 px wide. The owner chose "Both, raster first":
- **This run:** dither the graphic raster's gradients, inside the vendored tiny-skia.
- **Next run:** the compositor's 8-bit output dither (#375 part 2, already designed at `~/.claude/litecode/framejob/dither-375/01-spec.md`). Read that spec, and keep this run's choices consistent with it (pattern, amplitude, determinism) where they apply.
- **Deferred:** a deeper (16-bit) raster is #374. Do NOT do that here.

The design question, investigated by the designer:
- `graphic/` renders through resvg 0.48.1 on tiny-skia 0.12.0. tiny-skia evaluates gradients in its highp (f32) and lowp pipelines and rounds to u8 at store, with no dither stage. Skia proper has one.
- Vendor tiny-skia (e.g. `graphic/vendor/tiny-skia` through `[patch.crates-io]`, licence and provenance recorded) and add a dither stage applied to gradient paints (linear, radial, and the two-stop fast path) before store, in both pipelines or by forcing highp for gradient paints.
- Keep the patch as small as possible and documented, so it can be re-applied on a tiny-skia upgrade, or upstreamed.

Owner constraints, already settled:
- **Always on.** No setting, no module or prop switch, so there is no MCP mirror.
- **Deterministic.** The same module, frame and props always draw the same pixels. This is a stated graphics invariant (`docs/graphics-api.md`, "The same frame with the same props always draws the same pixels").
- **About ±½ level.** A colour exactly on an 8-bit level stays exact, so solid fills, text and logos are byte-unchanged and only gradient interiors move.
- **Static pattern.** It depends on pixel position, not on the frame, unless the design shows a reason otherwise. Then STOP with the options.
- **Not dithered:** non-gradient paints (solid fills, images, text) and alpha.
- Record the decision in spec §11 before the code: a new ID that amends PR-5. PR-5 itself stays (8-bit graphics); this adds dither within it.
- The graphics reference (`docs/graphics-api.md`, also served by `graphic_reference` and written to each package as `API.md`) says gradients are dithered.

Proof:
- Measure bands before and after on the #374 gradient, rendered through `render_graphic` and `render_frame` and decoded from an H.264 export: distinct levels, run lengths, monotone trend. Solid fills must be byte-unchanged.
- Every graphic proof and baseline that holds a gradient (`graphics_proof.py`, `graphic/tests/`, frozen references) is re-recorded or amended in the same change, and named in the §11 entry.
- Mutants for the new decisions.

EOF

I've set things up for raster first, then the output dither. Nothing is built yet: the raster-dither triage has just started in the background.

**Run 1: dither SVG gradients where they're drawn.** This is the fix for the bands you're seeing. tiny-skia, the library that rasterizes SVGs for graphics, gets a vendored patch adding a dither stage to its gradient pipeline, just before each pixel is rounded to 8 bits. The constraints:
- **Always on and repeatable:** no setting, and the same frame always draws the same pixels.
- **Only gradients:** the dither is about ±½ level and applies to linear, radial and two-stop gradients. Solid fills, text, images and alpha stay byte-identical.
- **Decision first:** a new spec §11 entry amends PR-5 before any code. Graphics stay 8-bit, now dithered.
- **Proof:** bands measured before and after on the promo's gradient, in a graphic render, a timeline frame and a decoded H.264 export. Any graphic baselines that contain gradients get re-recorded.
- **Integration:** fast-forward merge to main.

**Run 2: dither the compositor's 8-bit output.** Its design is done and the adversarial review found three problems for the revision to fix:
- `render_frame`'s scopes would end up measuring the dithered frame;
- one APNG check was set at a size the export never writes;
- three of the planned mutants have no change written for them.

The revision will be built on top of the merged raster dither.

Your decision is recorded on #375 and in the handoff files. #374 (16-bit rasters) stays deferred.

  **Where the dither goes**
  - tiny-skia 0.12.0 is vendored into `graphic/vendor/tiny-skia/`. The patch touches four files:
    - **`pipeline/mod.rs`:** a new `Stage::Dither` added as the last variant.
    - **`highp.rs`:** the stage itself.
    - **`lowp.rs`:** a `null_fn` entry, so any pipeline holding the stage compiles highp. That is how gradients are forced to highp.
    - **`shaders/gradient.rs`:** one line pushing the stage after the gradient's stages. That one line covers linear, radial, the two-stop fast path and the many-stop stage.

The raster-dither design is done and is now in adversarial review. It needed no decision from you.

- **The patch:** tiny-skia is vendored into `graphic/vendor/tiny-skia/` with a small four-file patch. A new dither stage is added once to the shared gradient setup, which covers linear, radial and multi-stop gradients. Gradients are moved onto tiny-skia's 32-bit float path so the stage has in-between values to work with. A test will measure how much that slows drawing.
- **The pattern:** a fixed per-pixel pattern of about ±7/16 of a level, the same in R, G and B, with alpha left alone. Colours already on an 8-bit level stay exact.
- **A trap the design caught:** the app's library is built from `core/`, and Cargo ignores a patch declared only in `graphic/`. The tests would have passed while the app shipped undithered. The patch is now declared in both places, and a `core/` test plus a mutant guard it.
- **Smaller than expected:** only the title-card pins in `graphic/tests/pins.json` contain a gradient, so they're the only baseline that moves. Shape-clip gradients aren't affected, because Core Graphics already dithers them.
- **Proof:** a new `raster_dither_proof.py` measures the bands before and after, in a graphic render, a timeline frame and a decoded H.264 export, using a reproduction of the promo's gradient. Solid fills must stay byte-identical to a control captured before the change. It also has 9 mutants.
- **Spec §11:** this becomes PR-13, amending PR-5. The output dither will be PR-14.

**Before this merges:** your licence edits touch `core/Cargo.toml` and `graphic/Cargo.toml`, and so does this patch, so main needs to be clean for the fast-forward merge. A conflict between the two would be trivial to resolve; I just need to know whether to commit the licence first.

The raster dither's design is final and implementation has started in the worktree. The revision accepted both review objections:
- **The exactness test:** its translucent case now uses `#326496` at 0.6 opacity. Once transparency is applied that comes out on whole levels, so a correct dither leaves it untouched. The spec's rule now reads "a premultiplied value on a level stays exact". It also states the limit: a translucent colour that falls between levels comes out as the two neighbouring levels, where a solid fill gives one.
- **The patch check:** the vendored tiny-skia is now compared to its recorded diff with one fixed command that drops timestamps. It was tested to produce a patch that applies cleanly.

The implementer starts by rebasing onto main, so the patch tables in `Cargo.toml` land after your licence line.

# Spec §11 — decisions: Foundations (M1–M3, road map 2)

Part of spec §11, *Decisions made — do not re-litigate*. The index of every decision is
[`README.md`](README.md).

- **AVFoundation, not ffmpeg.** Risk: MKV, WebM/VP9 and AV1-in-MKV do not
  open. Mitigation (M3, landed): an opt-in import step that shells out to a
  user-installed ffmpeg (present at `/opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg` on the
  development machine) to rewrap or transcode. The conversion is written to
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/Rewrapped/`, **not into the
  package**, for two reasons the `FFmpegRewrap.rewrapDirectory` comment
  spells out: opening an MKV from the Finder makes an UNTITLED document, so
  the import that needs a conversion is exactly the one with no package to
  put it in; and `fileWrapper(ofType:)` is a two-child whitelist whose one
  surviving location, `cache/`, is documented-regenerable (§5.6) — the last
  place for the only decodable copy of someone's footage. The name carries
  a digest of path, size and modification date, so a conversion is reused
  and invalidates itself. `RCFFmpegImport` chooses the policy and
  `RCFFmpegPath` the binary; with neither ffmpeg nor a cached conversion
  the import fails exactly as it did before the feature existed.
  Amended by #216-R: WebM and Matroska open by a built-in rewrap; ffmpeg
  remains the opt-in step for what that does not copy.
  Amended by #227: that step copies a constant-rate VP9 Profile 0 or 2
  video stream rather than re-encoding it, kept only when every frame of
  the copy is on its rate's grid.
  **Amended by NM-4** (rename R0):
  `~/Library/Application Support/Reelcut/Rewrapped/` is now
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/Rewrapped/`.
- **Custom compositor from day one** (M1 step 5). `AVVideoCompositing`
  has sharp edges — pixel-buffer pools, timing, `renderContextChanged`.
  Building the single-layer version first de-risks every later effect.
- **`AVPlayerLayer` under an overlay view**, not a self-driven `MTKView`,
  for the preview: A/V sync and scrubbing come from the player; the
  overlay maps through `videoRect`.
- **One JSON op entry point** (`rc_project_apply`) instead of one C
  function per op. Trade-off accepted: argument checking moves to
  Rust (`Err`) and to the typed Swift builders; in return the header is
  stable and the MCP catalog is the same table.
- **The plan-string compare** decides rebuild vs. refresh. Simple, and
  correct by construction because the plan contains exactly the
Apple M2 Max

Yes, but macOS can't do the encoding for us. Apple provides decoders for these formats on some Macs and no encoders on any, so Frame Job would need its own encoder.

**What I checked on this Mac (M2 Max, macOS 26.5.1)**
- **No AV1 or VP9 encoder exists in VideoToolbox.** The system's encoders are only H.264, HEVC (including alpha), ProRes, JPEG and H.263. That's true of every Mac: Apple's AV1 hardware on M3 and later decodes only.
- **No hardware decode here.** Neither AV1 nor VP9 reports hardware decode on this machine. That's the "depending on the machine" you've seen on import: AV1 only plays on M3 or later, and VP9 relies on macOS's own decoder.
- **AVFoundation can't write WebM at all.** VP9's usual home is WebM. AV1 normally goes in MP4.

**Ways to add it**

1. **Use ffmpeg, if the user has installed it.** This copies the import precedent in spec §11, where WebM/MKV conversion can shell out to an ffmpeg the user installed themselves. The export would feed frames to `ffmpeg` with SVT-AV1 or libvpx-vp9.
   - Cheapest by far.
   - The app stays free of ffmpeg.
   - It only works for people who have ffmpeg with those encoders installed.
2. **Bundle the encoders.**
   - **Libraries:** SVT-AV1 (BSD + AOM patent licence) and libvpx (BSD), both compatible with Apache-2.0, built into the app.
   - **Muxers:** AV1 needs an MP4 muxer; whether AVFoundation can carry AV1 samples is unverified, so this is a spike question. VP9 needs a WebM muxer, which would be new code. The core already reads Matroska but doesn't write it.
   - **Cost:** a real road map, plus build work for the C libraries.
   - **Alternative:** rav1e is a pure-Rust AV1 encoder, but it would break the architecture rule that Rust does no pixel work, so that would be your call.
3. **Either way, it's slow.** Encoding is software-only. SVT-AV1 at fast presets can roughly keep pace at 1080p; VP9 and high-quality AV1 are several times slower than real time. They'd suit the Export Queue, not quick previews.

**Is it worth it?** For uploads, not really: YouTube and most platforms re-encode anyway and take H.264 or HEVC happily. The strong case is **VP9 WebM with alpha**. It's the transparent-video format Chrome and Firefox play; Frame Job's HEVC-with-alpha only plays in Safari. Transparent graphics, like the ones the motion graphics engine makes, are exactly what people want to put on web pages. AV1 is mainly about smaller files for self-hosted web video, and good 10-bit HDR delivery.

My suggestion: file it as an issue now. If you want it, start with a short spike: the ffmpeg route end to end, whether AVFoundation can write AV1 into MP4, and a VP9-with-alpha WebM test against SVT-AV1/libvpx encode speeds on this machine. Then decide between the ffmpeg route and bundled encoders. Want me to file it, and should it go in Post Release?

Owner decision, 2026-10-27: Frame Job exports AV1 and VP9, with the encoders **bundled in the app**, not through a user-installed ffmpeg. "It is super valuable to me. Bundle the encoders."

## Why it needs bundling

Measured on an M2 Max, macOS 26.5.1, with `VTCopyVideoEncoderList`:
- VideoToolbox offers only these encoders: H.264, HEVC (also its alpha, depth and disparity variants), ProRes 422/4444/XQ, JPEG and H.263. There is no AV1 or VP9 encoder, and Apple's AV1 hardware on M3 and later decodes only.
- `VTIsHardwareDecodeSupported` is false for both AV1 and VP9 on this Mac.
- AVFoundation cannot write a WebM file.

Import already handles both formats: MP4 as is, WebM/Matroska through the built-in rewrap (#216, #227), and decode depends on the machine. Export does not.

## Scope, with the decisions still open

These go to a spike first, and the open choices come back to the owner:

- **AV1 encoder:** libaom (AOM's reference encoder, BSD-2 plus the AOM patent licence) or SVT-AV1 (BSD-3 plus the AOM patent licence). Measure speed and quality on Apple Silicon. rav1e (Rust) would break the "no pixel work in Rust" rule, so it needs the owner.
- **VP9 encoder:** libvpx (BSD-3), including VP9 with alpha in WebM. Chrome and Firefox play that as transparent web video; HEVC with alpha plays only in Safari.
- **Containers:**
  - AV1 in MP4: can `AVAssetWriter` write precompressed `av01` samples, or does it need a muxer of our own?
  - AV1 and VP9 in WebM: a Matroska *writer*. The core has only an index reader today.
- **Audio:** WebM carries Opus or Vorbis, not AAC, so that needs libopus (BSD-3). AV1-in-MP4 can keep AAC.
- **Depth and HDR:** 10-bit AV1, VP9 profile 2, HLG and PQ colour tags, to match the HEVC 10-bit and HDR rows.
- **Build:** each C library vendored or fetched at a pinned version, built for arm64 by the Makefile and Xcode, with provenance recorded. Their licences go in the acknowledgements (#376).
- **Speed:** software encodes run in the Export Queue. Measure 1080p30 throughput at the presets offered.
- **Product surface:** new export preset rows (spec §7.8 and §6's `export` tool, so the MCP mirror and the guide's export page), plus dist_check rows proving the libraries are in the bundle and signed.
EOF

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent.
