duration.description: Length, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default: the module's meta.durationInFrames at the canvas rate, else 5 s.

height.description: Height the module draws at, in pixels. Default: meta.height, else the canvas.

name.description: The module: graphics/<name>.js, lowercase letters, digits and -.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

props.description: The values to draw with, keyed by the schema's names; a key left out draws with the schema's default.

scope.description: Edit INSIDE a nest, by nest id — get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows. With it, every id in this call — clips, tracks, actions — is looked up in THAT nest's own tracks and clips instead of the timeline's, and every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero (a nest has no speed, so the whole mapping is t minus the nest clip's start); media ids are unaffected, because a nest shares the document's media. The op itself is unchanged and one call is still one undo step. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. Eight ops have no meaning inside a nest and refuse by name when you ask for one: add_marker, set_marker, remove_marker, set_canvas, add_media, relink_media, remove_media, add_adjustment_clip. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. The two that carry a TIME — add_marker, and set_marker with a time — are refused instead, because a marker is at project time while the playhead inside a nest is not, so the tick you would send means the wrong frame. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

width.description: Width the module draws at, in pixels. Default: meta.width, else the canvas.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_marker
tools.description: Drops a marker on the timeline. Markers snap to frames and two may not share a time, so a second marker on the same frame is refused. A chapter marker also becomes a chapter in the exported file (M2).

at.description: Where, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default: the playhead.

chapter.description: Also a chapter of the exported movie (default false).

color.description: Colour NAME, e.g. "red" — not a hex string.

name.description: Marker name. Default: Marker <n>.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

scope.description: Edit INSIDE a nest, by nest id — get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows. With it, every id in this call — clips, tracks, actions — is looked up in THAT nest's own tracks and clips instead of the timeline's, and every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero (a nest has no speed, so the whole mapping is t minus the nest clip's start); media ids are unaffected, because a nest shares the document's media. The op itself is unchanged and one call is still one undo step. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. Eight ops have no meaning inside a nest and refuse by name when you ask for one: add_marker, set_marker, remove_marker, set_canvas, add_media, relink_media, remove_media, add_adjustment_clip. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. The two that carry a TIME — add_marker, and set_marker with a time — are refused instead, because a marker is at project time while the playhead inside a nest is not, so the tick you would send means the wrong frame. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_text_clip
tools.description: Adds a text clip — a title. It has no source, so it can be any length; the default is 5 s of the Title preset, centred. Style it afterwards with set_text and place it with set_video (x, y, scale).

at.description: Start, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

duration.description: Length in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default 5 s (3000000).

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

text.description: The words, or the styling too. A plain string is shorthand for {"content": ...}; an object is a set_text patch merged over the Title preset. Text properties to merge. Keys: content, font (a PostScript name), size (px), color, align (left|center|right), valign (top|middle|bottom), line_spacing, tracking, outline (null or {width, color}), backdrop (null or {color, padding, radius}), width (null for auto-sizing, or a wrap width in px), animation (null or {kind: typewriter|word_fade|line_rise, in, out} — how the words arrive and leave. in and out are DURATIONS in ticks measured from the clip's own first and last frame, not times; either may be 0 for no ramp at that end, and in + out longer than the clip simply shows a partial reveal, and both are snapped to the document's frame grid. Like shadow and backdrop it MERGES: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {animation: null} clears the whole thing), case (as_written|upper — applied before layout; it never changes the word count), words (one {start, end} per whitespace token of content, in clip ticks, or [] for an untimed page — a content change that alters the count must send words: [] in the same patch), word_style (null or {mode: highlight|build, active_color, active_scale 1–1.5, active_pill {color, padding, radius, glide}, spoken_color, upcoming_color, active_fill, pause_dim 0–1} — how the word being said is drawn; it replaces animation. Three looks, each off by default: active_pill.glide (true|false) slides the pill from the word before to the active one over 0.2 s, or sooner when the next word starts sooner, instead of jumping; active_fill (true|false) fills the active word left to right from its start to its end, taking 0.6 s at most — the part said in active_color and the rest in upcoming_color, or not yet drawn in build mode; in highlight mode it shows only where those two colours differ; pause_dim fades the words and the pill to 1 − pause_dim of their opacity in a pause of 0.25 s or more — after one word's end until the next one's start, before a late first word, and after the last word until the clip ends — over 0.1 s each way, and outside 0–1 it is refused). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped. Default: the Title preset's placeholder.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_track
tools.description: Adds an empty track. INDEX 0 IS THE BACK of the layer stack — the bottom lane of the timeline, drawn first — and tracks.count is the front, which is what ⇧⌘N adds and where an overlay belongs.

index.description: Where in the stack (0 = back). Default: the front.

name.description: Track name, e.g. "Titles".

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__add_transition
tools.description: Makes an overlap at the HARD CUT before a clip and puts a transition on it — Clip ▸ Transition ▸ <kind> on a clip that abuts the one before it. The overlap is built out of material the two clips already have (the source before the incoming clip's in point, and after the outgoing clip's out point), so NOTHING else on the timeline moves and the pair's outer edges stay exactly where they were. duration is snapped down to whole frames and CLAMPED — to each side's available material, to the neighbours on the track, and to the overlap rule — so a request too long for the media lands shorter rather than failing; a request that clamps below one frame is refused. An affected track already outside the overlap rule is refused by that rule before fitting. align center takes half from each side (an odd frame goes to the incoming clip, and a side with nothing to give passes its share to the other), before takes it all from the incoming clip's head, after all from the outgoing clip's tail. kind absent uses the clip's stored kind if it has one and cross_dissolve otherwise; a stored transition keeps its curve and crossfade, a new one is eased at both ends and crossfades its sound. The incoming clip's actions move with its new first frame, so a zoom stays on the source frame it was drawn over. Errors when duration is not positive and when the clip is NOT at a hard cut, naming which of: no clip before it, a gap, an overlap that already exists (use set_transition or set_transition_duration for that one). With ripple true the overlap is made by MOVING instead — the sheet's Shift Clips Left button when neither clip has footage beyond the cut: no material is read and align is ignored, and the incoming clip plus every clip at or after the cut on every unlocked track slides left by duration, so the timeline gets that much shorter and no clip's source window changes. It is capped at half the shorter of the two clips and limited to the greatest whole-frame shift that leaves every moved track inside the overlap rule, including after clips cross; a clip on another track pushed into its neighbour gets a cross_dissolve; markers do not move.

align.description: Which side the overlap comes out of. Default center. Ignored with ripple.

duration.description: Requested overlap length, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Clamped, never refused for being too long.

kind.description: The transition. Absent uses the clip's stored kind, else cross_dissolve. Not nullable — set_transition clears.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

ripple.description: Make the overlap by sliding the incoming clip and everything after it left, for two clips with no footage beyond the cut. Default false.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__export
tools.description: Starts writing the timeline to a file and answers AT ONCE with {export_id, path, status} — ⌘E, the export sheet's six controls (format, size, frame rate, quality, loudness, range) in the sheet's own vocabulary, all but the frame rate — this exports at the document's rate, or on gif and apng at the format's own rate (12.5 and 25 fps). The export is a job in the Export Queue, run one at a time behind any other export already there; status is queued or running. Follow it with export_status, which never waits — call it again after a pause until status is done, failed or cancelled — and stop it with cancel_export. The export_id lasts until Frame Job quits. Every refusal comes back from this call, before anything is queued: a bad argument, a missing folder, and a graphic clip whose module does not compile; a failure while writing comes back from export_status, failed with its reason (a graphic that fails during the export stops it with no file left, naming the graphic and the frame). The preset is the ENCODING only and the size a separate choice defaulting to the document's own, or on gif and apng to the format's cap; the core resolves both into concrete settings (container, codec, size, rate, range) and hands them to the same exporter the sheet uses, so an agent export and a menu export cannot disagree. An existing file at the path is replaced, and the container's extension is added when the path has none. In an HLG project (set_canvas output) hevc_10bit, prores_422 and prores_4444 write HLG unless dynamic_range says pq or sdr, and every other video preset writes the project's SDR version. What the finished file holds is export_status's done answer.

audio_bitrate.description: Target AAC rate in BITS per second (192000 is 192 kbps) — the sheet's Quality popup. Omit for 192 kbps. Ignored where the sound is not AAC: ProRes, WAV and AIFF all write LPCM, whose rate is its sample format.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

dynamic_range.description: An HDR (HLG) project's picture on hevc_10bit, prores_422 and prores_4444 — the sheet's Dynamic Range popup: hlg (the default; BT.2100 HLG, no Dolby Vision), pq (HDR10: BT.2100 PQ at 1,000 cd/m2, mastering display P3-D65 0.005–1,000 cd/m2, MaxCLL 1,000, MaxFALL 0) or sdr (the SDR version). Every other video preset writes the SDR version; hlg and pq are refused there and in an SDR project, where sdr changes nothing.

loudness_lufs.description: Normalise the whole mix to this integrated loudness, in LUFS — the sheet's Loudness popup, whose rows are -14 (streaming), -16 (podcast) and -23 (EBU R 128 broadcast). The export measures itself first and then applies ONE gain to everything, so relative levels inside the timeline are untouched and no limiter is involved. Omit not to normalise: the export still measures and still reports. Ignored where there is no sound to measure (gif, apng).

path.description: Where to write, e.g. ~/Movies/cut.mp4. The folder must exist.

peak_dbtp.description: The true-peak ceiling that gain is capped against, in dBTP. The sheet fixes it at -1 and this is the knob for anything else. Because normalisation is gain-only, a ceiling with no loudness_lufs beside it would have nothing to cap and is REFUSED rather than accepted and left inert. When the ceiling bites, the file lands quieter than the target asked for and the result's capped_by_peak says so.

preset.description: Export preset id — one per encoding, a container and a codec with no size of its own (that is size's). h264 is what the export sheet opens on. Three rows keep a transparent canvas transparent: prores_4444 and hevc_alpha (the movie rows — see size, which constrains them) and apng. gif is not one of them: it can show a transparent pixel but has no alpha channel, so nothing partial survives it. prores_422, prores_4444 and hevc_10bit keep the compositor's 16-bit frames at 10 bits (ProRes 4444 at 12); h264, hevc and hevc_alpha are 8-bit. Pass a wrong one once and the error lists them all.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

range.description: What to write: the whole timeline (default), or just the in/out range set_range set — the sheet's Range popup.

size.description: Output size — the sheet's Size popup. A row id: document (the default, the document's own size, evened on the formats that need it), 1080p, 720p, 1440p or 2160p (the number is the SHORT edge and the long edge follows the document's aspect, rounded to even, so a vertical project's 1080p is 1080 × 1920), or preset for an image format's cap (gif and apng, where it is the default) — or an explicit [width, height] in px, the sheet's Custom.... Every row exists on every document — a 1920 × 1080 project's 1080p is its own size and is listed anyway — so an id means the same thing wherever it is sent; only preset is confined to gif and apng. Omit for the document size or the image format's cap; a wrong id's error lists the ids. A movie is written at exactly the size asked for, letterboxed if the shape differs by more than a pixel (within a pixel the picture fills the frame instead) — except on prores_4444 and hevc_alpha, where a size of a DIFFERENT SHAPE from the canvas is refused rather than written, because the padding destroys the alpha channel those rows are chosen for; every row id is already the document's own shape, so this only bites on a [width, height] of another shape. h264, hevc, hevc_alpha, hevc_10bit and prores_422 need even dimensions: an odd width or height — the document size on a canvas with an odd edge, or an odd [width, height] — is written one pixel smaller on that edge, and the width and height reported back are the file's. The shape is judged on that even frame: a [width, height] in the canvas's own proportions is never refused for being odd, at any scale; one of another shape is judged as the even size it becomes, which is the size hevc_alpha's refusal names. prores_4444, gif and apng keep an odd edge. On gif and apng a size — the cap, a row, or [width, height] — is a box the picture is fitted inside, aspect kept and never upscaled, and the width and height reported back are the file's: a vertical 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

video_bitrate.description: Target video rate in BITS per second (8000000 is 8 Mbps) — the sheet's Quality popup. Omit to let the preset's own encoder settings decide. Ignored by presets that carry no rate of their own: ProRes is fixed by its profile, and GIF and APNG have no bitrate at all.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__export_status
tools.description: How an export this launch started is going — Window ▸ Export Queue's row for it, read now: it never waits, so call it again after a pause. Always export_id, status (queued, running, done, failed or cancelled), path and elapsed (seconds since export was called, or to the finish once it has finished). running adds progress (0 to 1) and phase while the exporter names one (the loudness measurement). done adds what the file holds: ok, bytes, the settings that were used (preset, container, codec, width, height, fps [num, den], start, duration), burn_in_timecode, dynamic_range in an HLG project (the picture written), loudness for every format that carries sound, normalised or not — summary, integrated_lufs, true_peak_dbtp, sample_peak_dbfs, gain_db, ceiling_dbtp, capped_by_peak and target_lufs when one was asked, read off the mix that was written — and graphic_warnings [{name, frame, message}], each distinct warning a graphic gave while the file was drawn, absent when none. failed and cancelled add reason, the queue row's sentence. Only ids export returned are known, until Frame Job quits.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_graphic
tools.description: Reads the project's graphics/ folder. With name: that module's source, revision (the SHA-256 of its bytes), path, whether it compiles (ok, meta, schema, diagnostics), the clips drawn by it and kept, the revisions of its kept earlier texts, newest first (restore_graphic takes one). Without: folder, the folder's absolute path — where it WILL be when folder_exists is false; the first write_graphic creates it — and every module with its revision, ok and clips, warnings: what the folder's scan skipped or could not watch, in its own sentences, and history: [{name, kept}] for every name with a kept text, deleted modules included. The folder may also be edited with your own file tools: modules (<name>.js), fonts in fonts/ (.ttf, .otf) and pictures in assets/; the app sees a change within a moment. API.md and API.d.ts there are the reference, written by the app, and history/ is the app's too: the kept texts, which restore_graphic reads.

name.description: The module to read. Omit for the folder.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__get_project
tools.description: The whole project as JSON: canvas (width, height, fps [num, den], background, fit_new_clips, timecode_frames), media, tracks, clips and markers, with next_id — the schema every op edits. Plus the state that is deliberately NOT in the model and lives only in the app: playhead, selection and the in/out range. Read this first: every other tool names things by the ids it reports, and clip, track, marker and media ids share ONE number space, so an id is unambiguous on its own. tracks[0] is the BACK of the layer stack (the bottom lane of the timeline); times are ticks at 600000 per second. missing_media lists media whose file has moved — relink_media points it at the new one. graphics: every module in the package's graphics/ with its revision, whether it compiles, and the clips drawn by it.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__graphic_reference
tools.description: Answers the whole graphics API — the module's shape, ctx, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, limits and idioms — as Markdown, for an LLM to read once before writing a graphic. Needs no project open; a project, when given, must name an open one. Help ▸ Graphics Reference opens the same file.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_frame
tools.description: Renders one frame of the finished timeline as a picture so you can SEE the result — the verification hook. It goes through the same composition and the same Metal compositor an export does, so this is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it. The image comes back both as an image block and as a file on disk whose path the text names. Use it before and after every edit. It writes a PNG to a temporary file unless path or format says otherwise, so a call that names neither is exactly the call it always was. When a graphic in the frame warned or failed, a sentence before the last names the graphic, its frame and the diagnostic; a failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.

burn_in_timecode.description: Draw the project timecode over the picture, topmost — the export sheet's Burn in timecode checkbox. Default: false. It is a review copy's reference, so it reads the DOCUMENT'S timecode in the document's own spelling (the toolbar's, non-drop, HH:MM:SS:FF or HH:MM:SS.mmm), and it shows PROJECT time even in a file written from the in/out range: a range export starting at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 carrying a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00, which is the number a note about that frame needs.

format.description: The container to write. Default: the path's own extension when it is one of those (.jpg counts as jpeg), else png — so a call with no path and no format writes a PNG, as it always has. An explicit format WINS and the path's extension is REPLACED rather than appended to, so {path: "shot.jpg", format: "png"} writes shot.png. png and heic keep the canvas's alpha; JPEG has no alpha channel: a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

histogram.description: Also measure the frame's histogram, View ▸ Scopes' Histogram: R′, G′, B′ and Y′ counts per 256 levels. The text says what share of pixels clips high and low by Y′, and <image path>.histogram.json holds the four planes' counts and both percentages. Default false.

max_width.description: Cap the image's width in px, aspect kept and never upscaled. Default: the canvas's own size.

parade.description: Also measure the frame's RGB parade, View ▸ Scopes' Parade: R′, G′ and B′ each binned as the waveform bins Y′. The text says what share of pixels each channel clips high and low, and <image path>.parade.json holds the counts keyed red, green and blue (each 256 arrays by column bin, indexed by level) with each channel's clip marks and clip counts. Default false.

path.description: Where to write the file, e.g. ~/Desktop/shot.png. The folder must exist. Omit for a temporary file; either way the text block's last sentence names the file that was written. This is the same writer File ▸ Save Frame... uses, so a PNG written here and one saved from the menu are byte-identical.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

selection.description: An adjustment clip's id: draw what its video.qualifier selects instead of grading — grey, white fully graded, black untouched, times any matte cutting it, its strength not applied — with every layer in front of it left out; black where the clip is not on the frame. View ▸ Show Selection's picture; the view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Refused unless it names an adjustment clip. Default: none.

t.description: The moment to render, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid. Default: the playhead.

ungraded.description: Render as if no clip were graded — every clip's video.color (Light and Color) neutral, everything else kept: View ▸ Show Ungraded's picture. The view switch itself never reaches this tool or an export. Default false.

vectorscope.description: Also measure the frame's vectorscope, View ▸ Scopes' Vectorscope: Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral (bin 128). The text says what share of pixels is neutral, and <image path>.vectorscope.json holds the counts (256 arrays by Cr bin, indexed by Cb bin), the six 75 % targets' bins and the skin line's angle. Default false.

waveform.description: Also measure the frame's luma waveform, View ▸ Scopes' Waveform: the text says what share of pixels clips high and low, and <image path>.waveform.json holds the 256 × 256 counts (one array per column bin, indexed by level), the clip marks and both percentages. Default false.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__render_graphic
tools.description: Renders a module in graphics/ WITHOUT a clip — to look at it before placing it. png (the default) answers a contact sheet: the frames on a grid, each frame number printed under its cell, the cells scaled down (never the gaps or labels) so the sheet fits max_width; plus one sentence per frame that failed (drawn as its error card) or warned, with the engine's location. svg answers one frame's SVG text, its diagnostics and the ctx it was drawn with. ctx is a clip's: the canvas fps, durationInFrames from meta (else 5 s), the size from width/height, else meta, else the canvas. svg takes no path, background or max_width, which are the png sheet's, and writes no file. A frame at or past durationInFrames is drawn, with progress 1, as a longer clip draws it. A png sheet draws at most 134217728 px of frames (frames × width × height); past that the call is refused before any frame is drawn. No inspector control mirrors it: a person looks at the preview well.

background.description: What the png sheet is painted on: transparent (the default), checker, or a hex colour (#rgb, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa). Not with format svg.

format.description: png (default): the contact sheet. svg: one frame's SVG text.

frame.description: One frame to draw. Not with frames.

frames.description: The frames to draw, 1 to 16 of them, in order. Not with frame. Omit both for frame 0.

height.description: Height to draw at, in pixels. Default: meta.height, else the canvas.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__save_project
tools.description: Saves the project. A project that has never been saved — a new_project with no path, or a movie opened as one — needs a path; passing a path always writes there (Save As). Returns once the package is really on disk. A path another open project holds is refused; close_project closes that one first.

path.description: Where to write the .framejob package. Required the first time; otherwise the project is written back to its own file.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_action
tools.description: Moves or re-times an action, or changes its easing curve. Same overlap checks as add_action. Refused when the action would then end past the clip's end and later than it ended before, so an action already running past the clip's end (a trim can leave one there) can still be re-curved, moved earlier or shortened. When the action's end names a speed, the change moves how much source the clip reads, and one that would read past the end of its media is refused, naming the latest clip end that fits. Captions on a Captions track wholly inside a clip with sound are re-timed with it in the same step: captions_retimed lists them, and captions_removed those whose speech it no longer plays.

action.description: Action id (get_project lists each clip's actions).

curve.description: How the values ease from start to end.

duration.description: New length, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

scope.description: Edit INSIDE a nest, by nest id — get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows. With it, every id in this call — clips, tracks, actions — is looked up in THAT nest's own tracks and clips instead of the timeline's, and every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero (a nest has no speed, so the whole mapping is t minus the nest clip's start); media ids are unaffected, because a nest shares the document's media. The op itself is unchanged and one call is still one undo step. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. Eight ops have no meaning inside a nest and refuse by name when you ask for one: add_marker, set_marker, remove_marker, set_canvas, add_media, relink_media, remove_media, add_adjustment_clip. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. The two that carry a TIME — add_marker, and set_marker with a time — are refused instead, because a marker is at project time while the playhead inside a nest is not, so the tick you would send means the wrong frame. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

start.description: New start in CLIP time, in TICKS — 600000 per second, so 1 s = 600000 and one 30 fps frame = 20000. Rounded to the project's frame grid.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_action_end
tools.description: Sets what an action animates TO. The patch is the action's end state and MERGES into it key by key at every depth (a one-key shadow keeps the rest of it); a key set to null is REMOVED from the end state, so that property stops being animated. Groups are video, audio and text, with the same keys as set_video / set_audio / set_text — a colour is FOUR numbers here too, and it ramps in OKLab with straight alpha, as a graphic colour does; video.chroma.key's three numbers do too. A bad key or value is refused by its path with the group in it (video.filters[1].kind), though values are NOT range-checked: an animation may aim past what a stored property could hold. Two keys are refused: video.motion, a preset anchored to the clip's two ends rather than a value to ramp between (set it with set_video), and text.words, whose times belong to speech. A GRAPHIC clip's props are a fourth group, graphic: {props: {<key>: <value>}}, keyed by its module's schema and checked as set_graphic checks them, min and max included, against the module as graphics/ holds it NOW; the app reads that schema, so never send one. A number and a colour ramp along the curve: a number arrives with decimals (64 to 129 is 96.5 halfway), so a module that needs a whole number rounds it, and a colour blends in OKLab, as interpolateColors does, with straight alpha. A string, a boolean and an enum switch to the end's value when the action ENDS. An image (asset) prop switches to the end's image when the action ENDS; "" names no image there (null removes the prop from the end). A prop its module marks animate: false is refused: set it with set_graphic. A prop the clip holds no value for starts from the module's current default, written into the clip in the same undo step. graphic.props.<key>: null removes that prop from the end, graphic: null the whole group. get_project shows kinds beside props; the app writes it and ignores one you send, so an end read back can be sent again. While the module is missing or does not compile a prop value is refused (needs its module's schema) — get_graphic says why — and a null still removes. speed, a number beside the groups, is a MEDIA clip's rate (×0.1–×1000, clamped): the clip ramps from the rate in force to it along the curve and holds it after; the clip keeps its start and length and plays more or less source, and an end rate that would read past the end of its media is refused, naming the largest end rate that fits. speed: null removes it. Above ×12 the clip's audio is left out, and the answer carries audio_left_out and audio_note. With speed in the patch, captions on a Captions track wholly inside a clip with sound are re-timed with it in the same step: captions_retimed lists them, and captions_removed those whose speech it no longer plays.

action.description: Action id.

off.description: "group.key" paths (video.shadow, text.width) to switch OFF at the end — stored as null, where a null in patch removes. Optional keys only; never graphic.

patch.description: {video?: {...}, audio?: {...}, text?: {...}, graphic?: {props: {...}}, speed?: number} — the properties the animation ends at.

patch.description: Audio properties to merge. tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_graphic
tools.description: Patches what graphic clips are drawn from: name (another module), width, height, length (the graphic's own timeline in ticks; null ends it with the clip) and props, merged key by key — a null prop removes its key, except a key the module's schema has that an action on the clip animates (set_action_end's graphic): that one is set to the schema's default, so the animation keeps its start. A patch naming props or name is checked against the schema of the module it names, else of the one module every clip is drawn by; clips drawn by two different modules are refused for props. A clip that is not a graphic is an error. These are the BASE props; to animate one, add_action and then set_action_end.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_text
tools.description: Changes a text clip's words and typography. Merges like set_video; outline, backdrop and width set to null clear them (a null width restores auto-sizing). Position and scale are set_video's, not this tool's.

patch.description: Text properties to merge. Keys: content, font (a PostScript name), size (px), color, align (left|center|right), valign (top|middle|bottom), line_spacing, tracking, outline (null or {width, color}), backdrop (null or {color, padding, radius}), width (null for auto-sizing, or a wrap width in px), animation (null or {kind: typewriter|word_fade|line_rise, in, out} — how the words arrive and leave. in and out are DURATIONS in ticks measured from the clip's own first and last frame, not times; either may be 0 for no ramp at that end, and in + out longer than the clip simply shows a partial reveal, and both are snapped to the document's frame grid. Like shadow and backdrop it MERGES: a key you leave out keeps what is stored, and {animation: null} clears the whole thing), case (as_written|upper — applied before layout; it never changes the word count), words (one {start, end} per whitespace token of content, in clip ticks, or [] for an untimed page — a content change that alters the count must send words: [] in the same patch), word_style (null or {mode: highlight|build, active_color, active_scale 1–1.5, active_pill {color, padding, radius, glide}, spoken_color, upcoming_color, active_fill, pause_dim 0–1} — how the word being said is drawn; it replaces animation. Three looks, each off by default: active_pill.glide (true|false) slides the pill from the word before to the active one over 0.2 s, or sooner when the next word starts sooner, instead of jumping; active_fill (true|false) fills the active word left to right from its start to its end, taking 0.6 s at most — the part said in active_color and the rest in upcoming_color, or not yet drawn in build mode; in highlight mode it shows only where those two colours differ; pause_dim fades the words and the pill to 1 − pause_dim of their opacity in a pause of 0.25 s or more — after one word's end until the next one's start, before a late first word, and after the last word until the clip ends — over 0.1 s each way, and outside 0–1 it is refused). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_track
tools.description: Renames a track, flips its four switches — the track header's toggles, Track ▸ Hide Video / Mute Audio / Lock Track / Solo — or sets its matte, Track ▸ Matte. hidden drops its picture from the composition, muted its sound; locked keeps every ripple, insert and range edit off it; solo silences every OTHER track in its container (the timeline, or a nest's own tracks) that is not also soloed — mute wins on a track that is both, and pictures are untouched. matte makes the track a matte for the track directly behind it in its container: its clips are not drawn, and what they show cuts that track by alpha, inverted alpha, luma or inverted luma — where the matte track shows nothing, the track behind shows uncut; a back-most matte track, or one in front of another matte track, cuts nothing. Its clips still sound. "none" makes it an ordinary track again.

name.description: New track name.

tools.name: mcp__framejob__set_video
tools.description: Changes the clips' BASE video properties — position, scale, rotation, opacity, crop, corner radius, shadow, colour, chroma key, filters, reflection, spotlight and motion (what the clip does on its way in, on its way out and all the way through). The patch MERGES AT EVERY DEPTH: keys you leave out keep their values, inside a nested object too — a patch of just {shadow: {blur: 20}} keeps the shadow's colour, angle and distance — and shadow, chroma, reflection, spotlight or motion set to null clears it. A LIST is the exception: filters and obscure each replace whole, so send the whole stack and [] to clear it. A key or a value the vocabulary does not have is an error naming its dotted path (array indices included) and the value you sent; nothing is dropped, corrected or clamped. Placement is spec §5.3: the source rectangle is centred at the canvas centre plus (x, y), scaled, then rotated about that centre, and crop removes edges in place without shifting the content. To animate a property instead, add_action and then set_action_end. On an adjustment clip only color, wheels, curves, look, the point filters and opacity (the grade's strength) do anything, the qualifier narrows which pixels they reach, and blur, sharpen, pixelate or a blend mode is an error.

patch.description: Video properties to merge into the clip's base props. Keys: x, y (canvas px from the canvas centre, y DOWN), scale (1 = native pixels, 0.01–10), rotation (degrees, positive turns clockwise on screen), opacity (0–1), crop ({l, t, r, b} in SOURCE px — cropping never shifts the content), corner_radius (source px), shadow (null or {color, opacity, blur, angle, distance}), color ({brightness, contrast, saturation, hue, exposure, temperature, tint, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, vibrance, fade}, each 0 = unchanged and any subset merging — exposure is -3 to 3 (EV), fade 0–1 and the other seven tone keys -1 to 1, refused outside; a positive temperature is warmer, a positive tint more magenta; hue is in degrees, and a positive hue turns every colour's HSV hue that far, red → yellow → green, keeping its Rec. 709 luma), chroma (null or {key: [r, g, b], tolerance, softness, spill}), filters (an ARRAY of {kind, amount} applied in order, at most 4 — kind is blur|sharpen|pixelate|sepia|noir|vignette|invert and amount is 0–1; send the whole array, since it replaces rather than merges, and [] clears the stack), reflection (null or {opacity, height, gap, falloff} — height and falloff are fractions of the layer's cropped height, gap is source px), spotlight (null or {shape: rect|ellipse, x, y, width, height, feather, dim, zoom} — the centre and the box are SOURCE px from the cropped rect's centre, dim is how much darker it is OUTSIDE and zoom 1–2 magnifies what is inside), obscure (an ARRAY of {shape: rect|ellipse, x, y, width, height, feather, kind, amount} that HIDES what is under each one, at most 4 — kind is blur|pixelate and amount is 0–1, feather is the source px the effect ramps in over, and the centre and the box are SOURCE px from the cropped rect's centre, the same frame the spotlight uses. Like filters it is replaced whole rather than merged, so send the whole array and [] to clear it), blend (how this layer combines with what is already on the canvas: normal|multiply|screen|add|overlay|darken|lighten|difference — normal is source-over, which is what every project drew before this key existed. A blend needs something UNDER it: over the empty canvas multiply, darken and overlay read black while screen, add, lighten and difference change nothing, so add_background is usually the call before this one. It is forced to normal for the length of a cross dissolve, whose own weighting requires it, so what the frame shows there can legitimately differ from the value get_project reports), motion (what the clip DOES: null, or {in, out, during} — in and out are {kind: fade|zoom_in|zoom_out|slide_left|slide_right|slide_up|slide_down|spin|pop, duration: ticks} measured from the clip's first and last frame, during is {kind: pulse|shake|spin|bounce|drift, amount: 0–1, period: ticks} over the whole clip and drift ignores its period. Like every other object here it MERGES: a slot you leave out keeps what is stored, a slot set to null clears that slot, {motion: null} clears the whole preset, and a motion with no slot left reads back as null. The two durations are snapped to the document's frame grid and the period is snapped with a floor of ONE frame (it divides in every during formula and has no zero), so get_project can answer with a tick count near the one you sent rather than the one itself. in + out longer than the clip scales both down to meet rather than refusing. It is NOT an animation target — set_action_end refuses it — and get_project reports the clip UN-MOVED, since the preset becomes placement only when a frame is rendered), wheels ({lift, gamma, gain}, each {x, y, master}, each -1 to 1 and 0 = unchanged: x, y is the colour push, its angle the hue (0° red, 120° green, 240° blue) and its length the strength, and must lie inside the unit circle (x2 + y2 ≤ 1); master is the brightness; refused outside, never clamped. Any subset MERGES, so {wheels: {lift: {x: 0.2, y: -0.1}}} keeps lift's master and the other two wheels. Applied after color's tone and before look: lift moves black and holds white, gain moves white and holds black, gamma moves the middle and holds both ends), curves ({master, red, green, blue}, each a list of 2 to 16 [x, y] points, x strictly rising, x and y 0–1 inclusive; refused outside, never clamped. A list REPLACES that channel whole, null removes it, and a curve with every y = x from x 0 to x 1 is the identity, stored as no curve. Each channel is a monotone spline (Fritsch–Carlson) through its points, flat outside its first and last x; a colour is red(master(v)). Applied after wheels and before look. In an action's end an identity curve animates to neutral (an identity on either side takes the other curve's x's); two curves of different point counts blend their values across the action. Two hue curves too, hue_hue (Hue vs Hue) and hue_sat (Hue vs Sat): each 2 to 16 [hue, value] points, hue in degrees 0 ≤ hue < 360 strictly rising; hue_hue's value is a shift in degrees -180–180 (0 none) and hue_sat's a saturation gain 0–2 (1 none); a curve whose every value is its none is the identity, stored as no curve. Each is a periodic spline that wraps at 0/360. Applied after the channel curves and before look, at the colour's HSV hue read once: a positive shift turns HSV hue red → yellow → green keeping Rec. 709 luma, the gain scales saturation about that luma; a grey or near-grey (chroma at most 0.02) is left alone, and the effect fades in up to chroma 0.06), qualifier (adjustment clips only — anything else is an error naming the clip; which pixels the clip's grade reaches, read from the picture behind it BEFORE the grade: {hue: {center, width, softness}, saturation: {low, high, softness}, luma: {low, high, softness}, invert, blur}. hue is in degrees: center 0–360 (wraps), width 0–360 fully selected about the centre, softness 0–180 of fall-off outside each edge; a colour with chroma under about 0.06 has no hue and is never selected by it. saturation is HSV saturation (chroma / max, and near-black reads as 0) and luma Rec. 709 Y′, each low ≤ high and softness 0–1. A range MERGES: {hue: {}} turns hue on at {30, 50, 25} (saturation and luma at {0, 1, 0.1}), a partial range keeps the rest, null turns it off; the weight is the product of the ranges on, inverted by invert: true. blur 0–1 (0 off) softens that weight by a Gaussian of 24·blur canvas pixels, never the matte; it draws nothing with no range on. Refused outside the bounds, never clamped. In an action the numbers animate, the hue centre the short way round (350 to 10 passes 0); a range turned on or off and invert switch at the end. render_frame {selection: clip} shows what it selects), look (null, or {kind: warm|cool|teal_orange|vivid|faded|vintage|dramatic|black_white|lut, media, amount: 0–1} — one of the eight built-in looks, or lut: an imported .cube file, media its media id (import_media imports one), required with lut and refused with any other kind; applied after color and before the filters; amount is how much of it, 1 when left out, refused outside 0–1. It MERGES: a new kind keeps the clip's amount, a built-in kind replaces a LUT, an amount alone needs a clip that already has a look, and {look: null} removes it. In an action's end the amount animates and a change of kind or of LUT switches at the end). A colour is FOUR numbers, [r, g, b, a], each 0–1: three is refused by length and a component outside the range is refused by name, neither filled in nor clamped. chroma's key is the one exception, three numbers with no alpha.

project.description: Path of the open project to act on, as get_project reports it; omit for the frontmost one.

scope.description: Edit INSIDE a nest, by nest id — get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows. With it, every id in this call — clips, tracks, actions — is looked up in THAT nest's own tracks and clips instead of the timeline's, and every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero (a nest has no speed, so the whole mapping is t minus the nest clip's start); media ids are unaffected, because a nest shares the document's media. The op itself is unchanged and one call is still one undo step. Omit it to edit whatever the app has OPEN — the timeline, or the nest set_scope entered, exactly as an edit made by hand goes where the window is looking — so this argument is how you act on a container you are not looking at, and get_project always says which one you are in. Eight ops have no meaning inside a nest and refuse by name when you ask for one: add_marker, set_marker, remove_marker, set_canvas, add_media, relink_media, remove_media, add_adjustment_clip. The first seven behave DIFFERENTLY when the scope is inherited from set_scope rather than asked for here, and the result says which: five of them, plus set_marker's name / chapter / color and remove_marker, simply land on the DOCUMENT and are named under document_ops. The two that carry a TIME — add_marker, and set_marker with a time — are refused instead, because a marker is at project time while the playhead inside a nest is not, so the tick you would send means the wrong frame. Leave the nest (set_scope with no arguments) or pass the tick in project time. And read the result rather than assuming it landed: an edit can be perfectly valid inside the nest and still be refused for the whole DOCUMENT's sake, since the clip and track caps and the 8-deep nesting limit are counted across every container at once.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

Two things have happened since you approved the codecs.

**AV1/VP9: the spike has started.** I filed your decision as #377 and created a separate worktree, `~/devel/framejob-codecs`. A spike is now measuring:
- **Building the encoders:** whether libaom, SVT-AV1, libvpx and libopus build as arm64 static libraries, how long that takes and how much each adds to the app. It also looks at libwebm, Google's WebM muxer.
- **Speed and quality on this Mac:** encode speed at each preset, and quality against our HEVC at the same bitrate, at 8-bit and 10-bit.
- **Containers:** whether AVFoundation can carry AV1 and VP9 in MP4, and how to write WebM.
- **Alpha:** VP9 with transparency in WebM.
- **Audio:** Opus for WebM.
- **HDR:** the colour tags AV1 and VP9 need for HLG and PQ.

When it's done I'll bring you its recommendation and the real choices: which AV1 encoder, which containers, alpha, presets and HDR. libaom and libvpx are the natural picks given your brother's work, unless the numbers argue otherwise.

**Raster dither: it works, but a default H.264 export wipes it out.** The patched tiny-skia does what it should:
- in the graphic render and in `render_frame`, the median band shrank from 19 px to 2 px;
- solid fills stayed byte-identical;
- drawing was no slower (about 9 ms per frame before and after).

But the test exports a static one-second clip, and at default quality the H.264 encoder spent only about 60 kbit/s on it. That strips out the dither noise, so the steps came back. Since an H.264 export is exactly where you saw the bands, this matters.

A correction I owe you: I told the agents that ±½ level of dither, and "colours on a level stay exact", were your constraints. They were mine. A stronger dither is open if the numbers call for it.

Before asking you to choose, I've sent the implementer to measure the cases that matter:
- the same gradient moving, as in real video;
- H.264 at 8 and 16 Mbps;
- HEVC;
- ProRes as a reference that keeps the noise.

With those numbers the choice will be between three options:
- accept the limit for low-bitrate H.264;
- raise the default export quality so gradients survive;
- use a stronger, grain-like dither.

| ProRes 422 | **71 % less**; median band 19 px → 2 px | about 88 % of the dither noise survives |
| H.264 at default, 8 or 16 Mbps (still or moving) | 0–27 % less; static sometimes slightly worse | bands still 16–24 px median, 40–48 px widest |
| HEVC (8-bit) at default | 11 % less | same as H.264 |

Asking for a higher bitrate doesn't help. On smooth gradients Apple's encoder doesn't spend what it's given: the "16 Mbps" moving clip came out at about 0.6 Mbps. A ±7/16-level dither is cheap for it to throw away, and once it's gone, 8-bit H.264 has nowhere to put the in-between values, so the steps come back.

So the raster dither clearly fixes high-quality masters, but not 8-bit H.264 or HEVC at any bitrate this encoder will actually use. Before asking you, I've sent the implementer to measure two more cases:
1. **HEVC 10-bit.** I expect this to work. When the encoder smooths the dither away, the averaged values are the true in-between levels, and a 10-bit file can hold them.
2. **A stronger dither, ±1 and ±1.5 levels,** on moving H.264 at default and at 16 Mbps. It also measures how visible the noise becomes and what happens to colours that sit exactly on a level.

With those numbers the choice will probably be:
- fix it for ProRes and 10-bit exports only, which is what the dither already does;
- also add a stronger, grain-like dither so 8-bit H.264 holds up, at the cost of visible fine noise and some file size.

If 10-bit HEVC works, there's a third option: export your high-quality deliverables as HEVC 10-bit. They play everywhere modern, and YouTube accepts them.

Somewhat, for 8-bit. The bigger win is 10-bit output.

I re-encoded the dithered ProRes master (3 s, the static worst case) with each encoder and measured how much stair-step remains along the gradient. Lower is smoother. A plain undithered 8-bit staircase scores about 0.29.

| Encoder | Stair-step | Dither noise left | Size (3 s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ProRes master (reference) | 0.09 | 0.22 | — |
| Apple H.264, hardware, 8 Mbps (what Frame Job uses) | **0.44** | 0.08 | 1.4 MB |
| Apple H.264, software, 8 Mbps | 0.31 | 0.41 | 1.9 MB |
| x264, CRF 18 | 0.26 | 0.53 | 236 KB |
| x264, CRF 18, `tune grain` | 0.25 | 0.59 | 88 KB |
| SVT-AV1, 8-bit | 0.30 | 0.42 | 44 KB |
| **SVT-AV1, 10-bit** | **0.11** | 0.02 | 9 KB |
| **libvpx VP9, 10-bit** | **0.11** | 0.00 | 8 KB |

What it shows:
- **Apple's hardware H.264 encoder is the worst case.** It scores worse than an undithered staircase, adding blocking on top of the steps.
- **Software 8-bit encoders do better, but not well.** x264 keeps more of the dither, but only gets to about 0.25, still far from the master. And x264 is GPL, so it can't be bundled into an Apache-2.0 app. Apple's own software H.264 encoder can be, but only gets to 0.31 and is slower.
- **10-bit encoders basically match the master.** AV1 and VP9 smooth the dither away like the others do, but a 10-bit file can hold the averaged in-between values, so the gradient comes out smooth, and in tiny files.

So for 8-bit H.264 there's no encoder setting that really fixes it: 8 bits can't hold sub-level detail through lossy compression at sensible bitrates. The real fix for high-quality deliverables is **10-bit output**: the AV1 and VP9 10-bit export you've just approved, and probably HEVC 10-bit, which already exists. The implementer is measuring HEVC 10-bit now, along with a stronger grain-like dither, in case 8-bit H.264 still matters to you.

This was one quick run on a static clip, using a metric I wrote for it; the implementer's measurements are the controlled version.

Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste.
